item.title: U.N. General Assembly Set to Snarl Traffic, City Leaders Say
item.description:
Representatives from nearly 200 countries will descend on New York City this week as leaders converge on Midtown East in Manhattan for the annual session of the United Nations General Assembly, bringing motorcades — and therefore, traffic — with them.

“I know that, for many New Yorkers, the General Assembly is more synonymous with questions around traffic,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference last week. “When the world visits New York City, our streets are inevitably impacted.”

In addition to planned street closures for the entire week, there will also be rolling closures as delegations travel across the city.

Here’s what you need to know:

Midtown!

There are no known specific threats to this year’s General Assembly, Jessica Tisch, the police commissioner, said. Still, officers will secure hundreds of motorcades as heads of state and high-ranking officials move between hotels, U.N. buildings and meetings around the city.

“This is one of the most complex security operations that we carry out,” she said. “As always, there will be security measures that you will see and others that you will not see.”

A gridlock alert is in place from Sept. 21 to Sept. 25, Mr. Mamdani said. Rolling pedestrian and vehicle closures will take place around the United Nations Headquarters, spilling out across the city as delegations traverse the city. Portions of F.D.R. Drive will be closed, and ferry service will be disrupted, the mayor said.

Ms. Tisch said that from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26, First Avenue will be closed between 41st and 48th Streets, while 44th Street to 47th Street will be closed between First and Second Avenues. Each day until the end of the session, around 9 p.m., 42nd Street will close between First and Second Avenues.

The 42nd Street exit from F.D.R. Drive will also be blocked off. The Police Department said closures on parts of the F.D.R. will occur as needed.

The mayor recommended that commuters use public transportation.

“I want to thank New Yorkers in advance for their patience,” Mr. Mamdani said.

Each year, there is an uptick in protests related to the General Assembly, Ms. Tisch said. Those protests are generally contained to Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza on East 47th Street, but can grow to affect other parts of the city.

This year, protests are planned throughout the week, including demonstrations at Bryant Park, at Union Square and in Brooklyn.

“As always, the N.Y.P.D. will facilitate First Amendment activity,” Ms. Tisch said. “At the same time, there will be no tolerance for violence or destruction of property.”

item.title: An Unused and Divisive Philippine Nuclear Plant Awaits Its Fate
item.description:
Noel Germano leads the way through the dark, airless hallways of the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, an isolated compound west of Manila that was meant to be the first source of atomic energy in the Philippines. Instead of the thrum of massive turbines and steam generators, there is eerie silence: The plant has been mothballed for decades.

A yellow radiation protection suit is only for display, unneeded by Mr. Germano, who manages the plant, or any of his seven engineers as they go about the Sisyphean task of manually turning thousands of analog dials, switches and gears to prevent decay.

The plant was heralded by President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. in the 1970s as a step into a prosperous, modern era for the Philippines. Of its four planned reactors, only one unit was completed, in 1984, and it was never switched on. Decades later, his son — who was elected president in 2022 — has revived the country’s pursuit of atomic energy and his government is exploring options including potentially reviving the plant in Bataan.

The hulking concrete structure sits on an 800-acre site fenced off from the small seaside town of Morong. The plant’s grounds are still well maintained, but its interior, with the reactor that was designed to produce 621 megawatts, resembles a museum diorama. Bringing it to life is not impossible, but it is a tall and expensive ask, experts say.

The goal is the same now as it was in the ’70s: energy security. The elder Marcos, a dictatorial leader who was in power from 1965 to 1986, wanted to diversify the Philippines’ energy sources to guard against global oil shocks like the one in 1973. His son, Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr., has had to deal with similar fallout from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Reviving the Bataan plant might prove a hard sell in a cash-strapped country, especially to the Filipinos who see it as a reminder of the corruption and repression of the Marcos Sr. era. And the threat of nuclear catastrophe feels immediate for many residents of Morong, about a mile up the coast.

The project has never been free of skepticism, facing a number of questions from the beginning: Does the Philippines have enough expertise to run a nuclear power plant safely? Is it wise to build one in a part of the world where earthquakes and tsunamis are a constant threat? Can the country even afford it?

The elder Mr. Marcos’ government managed to secure financing for the plant through debt. Hundreds of engineers and technicians were sent abroad for training to build up a work force capable of running a nuclear facility.

The site, on a peninsula across the bay from Manila, was chosen because there was abundant water to cool the reactor and it was considered high enough to be safe from tsunamis, a constant threat because of frequent earthquakes in the region.

Construction began in 1976, bringing a windfall for the many people in Morong and other nearby towns who were hired to work on the project. They included Valentino Tolosa, who said he could not believe his luck when, at the age of 18, he got a job as a cable puller. It paid about $27 a day, ten times the allowance he got from his mother, he said.

Three years into the plant’s construction, more than 8,000 miles away in Pennsylvania, a reactor at Three Mile Island suffered a partial meltdown in what remains the worst nuclear energy accident in U.S. history. It turbocharged the antinuclear movement in the Philippines, whose activists came to Morong regularly to campaign against the plant being built nearby.

Rumors also spread across the Philippines in the 1970s that the site was particularly dangerous because it sat above a fault line, and was less than 40 miles from Mount Pinatubo, an active volcano. Researchers from the Philippine Department of Science and Technology have since found no active fault lines under Bataan, and the site was unharmed by the volcano’s most destructive eruption in 1991.

The first Marcos government, which displayed little tolerance for dissent, came down hard on the plant’s opponents.

Pilar Nazareno, a resident of Morong, said dozens of her neighbors who had questioned the nuclear project at the time were taken by the police or labeled communists by the government. Some residents pretended to attend Bible studies at a local church as cover for discussions about the plant, she said.

“It fell to the priests and nuns to teach us about the nuclear plant, and what would happen to us if it had a meltdown,” said Ms. Nazareno, 68.

The Three Mile Island accident led the Philippine authorities to suspend construction at Bataan in 1979 for a safety review. The design was updated and work resumed the next year, but safety was just one of the criticisms: Mr. Marcos faced persistent allegations of corruption related to the project, including that the American company Westinghouse had given him millions of dollars in illegal payments to secure a contract to build the plant.

By the time it was completed in 1984, the plant’s cost had more than doubled to over $2 billion. It took another two decades for the government to pay off the accumulated debt.

Mr. Marcos by then was struggling for his political survival. In February 1986, he was overthrown and fled the country. With its biggest backer out of office, the nuclear plant’s future was thrown into doubt.

“When the government changed, we already knew nothing would move forward at the plant,” said Antonio Corpuz, a chemical engineer who was appointed the plant’s manager in 1978.

Two months after Mr. Marcos’ ouster, a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in the Soviet Union, in what became the world’s worst nuclear accident. It left little appetite in the Philippines for the Bataan project. A new government mothballed the plant in April that year, and sold its uranium fuel to other countries.

The site’s two backup generators were taken away to provide power to remote islands. Radiation detectors were also removed from the security posts because they were not needed: There was no nuclear material at the plant.

Mr. Corpuz and his team, instead of overseeing power generation, were tasked with preserving the plant. And in the 1990s, hundreds of engineers left after the government cut its maintenance budget, leaving only enough for a skeleton crew. Many went to the United States, Japan, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates for higher-paying jobs.

Today, the only part of the plant that appears pristine is the reactor room, a 164-foot-high cylindrical structure with steel-reinforced, three-foot-thick concrete walls. The structure protects the reactor core, which sits in a deep well that would be filled with water if the plant were operational. Many components in the core are still wrapped in plastic.

Supporters of the Bataan plant have pointed to reactors of the same design in the United States and South Korea that have run safely for decades.

Mark Cojuangco, a member of Congress and a champion of the Bataan plant, said the Philippines had missed an opportunity by mothballing the project. “We could have built factories like South Korea and leaped ahead of the region,” said Mr. Cojuangco, whose father was a tycoon close to Mr. Marcos Sr.

The younger Mr. Marcos has appeared mindful of the Bataan plant’s history and the long-running skepticism about its safety and usefulness, often avoiding direct mention of the project.

In 2024, his government commissioned a study by the Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power Company on the feasibility of reviving the plant. The Energy Department of the Philippines said in July that the study had been completed, but declined to provide its findings. A 2017 study by the same South Korean company found that about a quarter of the plant’s equipment would need to be replaced before it could be switched on, at a cost of about $1 billion.

Mr. Marcos had aimed for the Philippines to start generating nuclear power by 2032, but the Energy Department told reporters in July that it might take until 2038 as the agency evaluates other options, including plants at different sites. A 2024 survey commissioned by the Energy Department found more than 70 percent of Filipinos in favor of nuclear power.

If the government decides in favor of the Bataan plant, the refit is still expected to take years.

Mr. Germano, the plant’s manager, said he doubted he would see it switched on in his tenure. He retires in 2030.

item.title: Hundreds of Drones Target Moscow on Final Day of Russian Elections
item.description:
Moscow and its surrounding region came under attack by hundreds of drones, the local authorities said on Sunday morning, killing two people and injuring 20.

About 1,600 drones heading toward the Moscow region were shot down, the Russian capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said, including 450 that had been approaching the city. An oil refinery and a warehouse were struck in the attack.

The attack came on the final day of parliamentary, regional and local elections across Russia. Russian officials have repeatedly said they are holding these votes under attack, possibly an implicit criticism of Ukraine, which has not held elections since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 because martial law forbids them. President Vladimir V. Putin has repeatedly criticized Kyiv and President Volodymyr Zelensky for not holding a vote.

Mr. Zelensky posted on Facebook that the bombardment included the first use of a newly developed Ukrainian ballistic missile to strike inside Russia. That missile does not have the range to reach Moscow, according to its manufacturer, Fire Point, so would have been aimed elsewhere in Russia.

The night was deadlier in Ukraine, where seven people were killed in strikes in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, according to Ukrainian authorities. Air alerts were on and off all night though most of the country.

Moscow’s mayor said “a few drones” struck the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya, which had been taken out of commission by attacks in June. At the time, it was estimated that the repairs would last for six months. On Sunday, Mr. Sobyanin said the refinery had again been damaged.

In the neighborhood of Ramenskoye, a 21-story building caught fire, and 600 residents were evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov.

A warehouse in the Moscow region was also struck, though no casualties were reported. For months, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses in Russia with long-range strikes.

All four airports in the Moscow region introduced temporary restrictions at the time of the attacks, and more than 30 flights were grounded, according to the newspaper Kommersant.

On Saturday, Mr. Sobyanin reported that a total of 2,022 drones had flown toward the Moscow region over the preceding seven days, 186 of which were shot down as they approached Moscow. Most of the drones had been shot down while they were still far from the city.

President Trump said last Monday that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to stop campaigns of pounding one another’s energy infrastructure but neither side has confirmed that an agreement had been reached. The attacks have continued through the week.

The outcome of the Russian elections looks to be a foregone conclusion: victory for the ruling party that supports Mr. Putin, because the Kremlin has engineered the vote to minimize competition.

Russians dread what may come after the Kremlin receives what most expect will be its desired result at the ballot box — whether that be another, albeit quieter, round of mobilization, more tax rises or more internet restrictions.

The country is already facing widespread fuel shortages because of Ukraine’s attacks on refineries. While fuel lines have become commonplace in the last few months, there were few on Saturday because not many fuel stations had any gas to sell. When they had something, it was low-quality gas or diesel.

In his statement on Facebook, Mr. Zelensky said the Ukrainians had struck with several types of domestically made drones and missiles created during the war in response to Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. These included Fury, FP-1 and Flamingo exploding drones, the Palianytsia cruise missile and the FP-7 Pelican ballistic missile, Mr. Zelensky said in the statement.

The Pelican missile is already in production in Ukraine, along with a larger, longer-range version expected to enter combat tests later this fall. The longer-range version, the FP-9, could reach Moscow.

item.title: On a Dot of France Off Canada, Carney and Macron Talk Partnership
item.description:
As part of Canada’s effort to knit closer ties with Europe, Prime Minister Mark Carney flew on Sunday to a French island just a ferry ride off Canada’s Newfoundland coast to meet with France’s president, Emmanuel Macron.

The brief encounter on St. Pierre, part of a speck of French territory in North America, comes before the opening of the United Nations General Assembly and days after the European Union invited Canada to become an “associate member.”

Neither leader offered any further details about that offer. (Associate membership is not a category that currently exists in the bloc.) But both men made it clear that the idea is a response to the breakdown in each’s formerly close relations with the United States, brought on by President Trump. Neither Mr. Macron nor Mr. Carney mentioned the president by name.

Instead, Mr. Macron highlighted interests that France and Canada share that the Trump administration rejects.

“We both believe that our two countries are strong, independent nations that wish to remain that way,” Mr. Macron said in a speech following a private meeting. “We both believe in democracy, in the respect for international law, and for free and fair trade, science on which rests our decisions, and of course, the strategic issues around which we work.”

Mr. Carney, for his part, said that “the time has come to tighten our ties.”

“Canada and Europe will build an alliance for the future that will strengthen our collective resilience so we can live the lives we choose, based on the values that we share across Fortune Bay,” he added, referring to the body of water that separates St. Pierre from Canada’s Newfoundland.

Last week Mr. Trump said that a closer relationship between Canada and Europe could be perceived as “a hostile act.”

Mr. Trump has expanded his trade war with Canada by imposing additional 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports and by banning the entry of some Canadian products. The moves followed the collapse of trade talks between the countries. Mr. Carney has attributed the failure to unacceptable demands from the United States, while Trump administration officials blamed Canada for making last-minute demands.

The president has also continued his social media slights against Canada, including recent posts of maps that overlaid the American flag on Canada, as well as on St. Pierre and the neighboring French island of Miquelon.

In a speech to the European Union last week, Mr. Carney said that a stronger alliance with Europe would preserve Canada’s sovereignty and freedom amid a “ferocious storm.”

The only thing certain about the invitation for associate E.U. membership is that it cannot be full membership. Aside from the E.U.’s legal requirement that members must be in Europe, it would likely be impossible for Mr. Carney, or any other Canadian leader, to sell Canadians on the idea that the best way to protect their sovereignty from American aggression would be to give some of it up to Europe.

And some Europeans — as well as Mr. Carney — appear uncomfortable about using the word “member” at all to describe the new partnership.

Canada and Europe already have a free-trade agreement, so little would be likely to change there. Analysts speculate that the new relationship could align some regulations, make it easier for some people (likely students) to move between continents, or strengthen the ties of financial services across the ocean. Mr. Macron and Mr. Carney both mentioned working together on A.I.

After quickly returning to Ottawa Mr. Carney met in Ottawa with Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store of Norway, a country with expertise on special arrangements with the E.U.

After Norwegians twice rejected joining Europe in referendums, it is now part of the European Economic Area. That leaves Norway subject to many European regulations, without having any say in how they are implemented. It also contributes money to E.U. funds intended to equalize economic and social programs throughout the continent. Norwegians can travel passport free to E.U. countries.

Afterward, the two men had little to say to reporters regarding any discussion they may have had about Canada joining Europe. Instead they focused on the growing connections between Canada and Norway, which Mr. Carney visited in March. In what Mr. Carney described as Canada’s largest military procurement in its history, his government said in July that it will buy a fleet of submarines from a Norwegian-German joint venture.

When asked by a reporter if Mr. Trump could also see a closer Norwegian-Canadian relationship as a “hostile act,” Mr. Carney said that “deeper ties between NATO allies makes those NATO allies stronger, makes NATO stronger and helps to achieve the common goals of all NATO members very much, the United States included.”

item.title: Parts of Britain Are, Once Again, Hit by Flight Delays
item.description:
Some travelers and airlines in Britain faced a cascade of flight delays on Monday, less than two weeks after a failure in an air traffic control system caused chaos at several airports in the country.

The disruptions on Monday mostly affected travelers in northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, including at airports in Manchester, Glasgow and Belfast.

National Air Traffic Services, the operator which provides most of Britain’s air traffic control services, said in a statement on Monday that it had “experienced a technical issue” at a Scottish center, which it described as a “connectivity issue with part of our systems network.”

By midmorning, the operator said the issue had been “fixed,” adding that it had “nothing to do with the problem we had earlier this month.”

Critics across the British transport sector responded with exasperation to the delays. Several airlines expressed concerns that National Air Traffic Services, or NATS, was ill-equipped for the task.

“Yet another NATS failure,” Tim Alderslade, the chief executive of Airlines UK, which represents major British airlines, said in a statement. He said that the country’s air traffic control system “is critical national infrastructure and it must be resilient enough to keep people moving.”

Travelers in the London area appeared to have been spared the worst of the delays. London City Airport, a small airport in the capital, said it was experiencing “some disruption.” Gatwick said that “a small handful of flights may face delays” but that it was “operating as normal.” There were no online reports of flight delays at Heathrow, which did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

“I know this will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue,” Heidi Alexander, the British transport secretary, said on social media, calling the snarl on Monday “a further IT issue” with National Air Traffic Services.

The delays on Monday appeared to be smaller than the chaos in Britain earlier this month, which led to the disruption of about 2,000 flights and upended long-planned vacations and work trips.

The disruptions came as NATS faces heightened scrutiny and criticism across the British transport sector over the flight delays earlier this month and over several other high-profile incidents, including a system fault in August 2023 that forced hundreds of cancellations.

Jet2, a budget airline, called the delays “unacceptable,” and said it would seek compensation from NATS. “It is simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down,” Steve Heapy, the chief executive of Jet2, said in a statement on Monday.

EasyJet, the budget airline, said in a statement on Monday that the incidents involving NATS called into question “the resilience of NATS’ systems.”

Monday’s delays came just three days after NATS published a preliminary report into the disruptions earlier this month.

Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of NATS, said in a statement on Friday that those disruptions were not related to the major system outage in 2023. Instead, he blamed a “software issue” in a flight data system and dismissed any speculation that it could have been “caused by military intervention,” like a cyberattack.

NATS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday about the criticism prompted by that day’s disruptions and about how long the technical issue lasted.

In Scotland, Glasgow Airport warned midmorning on Monday of “further disruption” because of “the knock-on impact across the network.” The Highlands and Islands Airports, which oversees 11 regional airports, said that the NATS issue had been resolved but that “some disruption may continue.”

Ryanair, another budget airline, called for the removal of Mr. Rolfe, the NATS leader. In a statement, Ryanair said that the operator’s reassurances after the disruptions earlier this month “have already been proven worthless.”

“Today’s disruption raises serious questions about NATS’ operational resilience and why, after repeated system failures, there is still no effective backup system capable of preventing widespread passenger disruption,” the airline said.

item.title: U.N. Seeks Relevance on A.I. as the U.S. and China Race Ahead
item.description:
As the threats posed by artificial intelligence spark international alarm, the stakes of the Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington this week have only grown bigger.

Earning considerably less attention are the meetings focused on A.I. at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, as world leaders gather in the shadow of several rogue A.I. hacking episodes that have prompted greater fears.

A.I. will be a dominant theme for a fleet of U.N. meetings on Monday centered on international digital cooperation. The schedule includes discussions about the technology’s risks and opportunities, the potential for economic dislocation and possible international governance.

Mr. Xi is expected to skip the General Assembly to instead convene in Washington with President Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed A.I. safety concerns as a hoax.

There is no shortage of tension between the two countries, and A.I. is just one of several issues the two sides are expected to discuss. But few issues are as contentious right now — or as important to humanity, some say — as the race for A.I. dominance.

The United States has repeatedly accused Chinese A.I. firms of stealing the intellectual property of American A.I. labs. China, too, continues to agitate against U.S. restrictions on advanced computer chips needed to power A.I. models.

Some onlookers, though expecting little, compared the urgency for a breakthrough on A.I. safety issues between the world’s two superpowers to the need for nuclear arms control agreements during the Cold War.

The U.N. gathering and the White House meeting underscore how much A.I. has become a race solely between two rival powers, with the rest of the world largely pushed to the periphery, foreign policy experts said.

“The U.N., to put it bluntly, has been sidelined in the A.I. conversation,” said Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies U.S.- China relations and focuses on technology issues.

A.I. is “a two-player game,” Mr. Chan added. “It’s kind of like nuclear weapons: If you do not have them or are not on the verge of having them, it’s hard to be relevant in shaping the discussion.”

Reflecting that reality, the United States and China discussed on Sunday creating a notification system to allow for the countries to alert each other about A.I.-driven national security risks. The mechanism, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, would be called “the U.S.-China A.I. dialogue.”

It is not for lack of trying. António Guterres, the U.N. secretary general, pushed last week for international cooperation on A.I., highlighting it as one of three existential risks facing humanity alongside climate change and deepening global inequality.

A.I., he said, presents other dangers, including amplifying misinformation, discrimination, privacy violations, cyberattacks and so-called superintelligence that could advance beyond human control.

“We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure and responsible development of A.I., while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards,” Mr. Guterres said. “The world cannot afford a race to the bottom on A.I. safety.”

Under Mr. Guterres, the United Nations has been trying to build international consensus around responsible A.I. development for years, including by forming an advisory body in 2023 to study the issue. And on Monday, the leaders of 22 countries adopted a declaration calling to strengthen “human direction, oversight and control” of A.I. systems. The United States and China did not join the declaration.

The two countries have only further cemented their leads ahead of everyone else since the U.N. began worrying about A.I., rushing to build out data centers and release cutting-edge A.I. models despite growing fears about existential risks associated with the technology.

In his remarks last week, Mr. Guterres acknowledged that “geopolitical divides” made policing A.I. difficult but said that voluntary pauses on the technology would not work if not everyone agreed to them — meaning, right now, the United States and China.

China had generally been seeking to increase its influence with the United Nations, but this summer launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which has its headquarters in Shanghai, in a bid to assert global dominance on international A.I. discussions. The United States has shown little interest in building international consensus on A.I. or other geopolitical matters.

The U.N. Security Council may hold more sway on A.I. than the General Assembly. The OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman will speak to the Security Council on Wednesday, a company spokeswoman said. But it is difficult to imagine the Security Council — on which the United States, China and Russia sit — forging a consensus, experts said.

Mr. Altman’s appearance at the United Nations is just a warm-up. A day later in Washington, he will join a far larger roster of A.I. and technology leaders for the U.S.-China state dinner, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Julian Ku, a professor of constitutional and international law at Hofstra University, said that the United Nations has always struggled to influence superpowers on the uses and limits of weapons they have that others do not, from nukes to high-powered hacking tools.

In the context of nuclear weapons, that took the form of helping nonnuclear nations gain access to nuclear power while spreading nonproliferation agreements, Mr. Ku said. While the United Nations would like to steer the A.I. safety conversation, it will probably find more success working to ensure the rest of the world is not fully left behind on the benefits societies could reap from the technology, Mr. Ku added.

“In a lot of ways, this is the story of the U.N. from the outset,” Mr. Ku said. “The U.N. can’t really shape the actions of those who have the power directly, but they do have the interests of everyone else who do not have that power.”

item.title: A Power Shift in America?
item.description:
When President Trump won a second term, he didn’t just win the presidency. The Republican Party he leads also retook the Senate and kept control of the House of Representatives. This control of both the executive and the legislative branches has given him a pretty free hand to do what he wants without meaningful pushback. Like start a trade war. And a real war.

But in six weeks, that could change. That’s when the United States holds midterm elections. All the seats in the House and a third of the seats in the Senate are up for grabs. My colleague Nate Cohn, our polling wizard at The New York Times, has looked at all the data points and says that, on paper at least, the Democrats have a real chance of winning big.

By Nate Cohn

Last week, a new New York Times/Siena poll found that the conditions for a so-called wave in November’s midterm elections might be coming into place. The only question is whether Democrats will be able to ride it.

Overall, Democrats lead Republicans, 51 percent to 43 percent, among likely voters asked which party they will support for Congress in their district.

That’s “blue wave” territory. At least in terms of the national vote, the Democratic margin in the poll — 8.5 points — would almost exactly match the party’s 8.6-point margin in 2018, when the Democrats regained control of the House of Representatives in Trump’s first term. And it would exceed the winning margins for the party out of power in other recent wave elections, like in 1994, 2006 and 2010.

The Times/Siena poll is just one survey, and polls are imprecise and subject to many sources of potential error. But this is also far from the only data point showing a major Democratic advantage.

The results are almost exactly in line with the average of other polls. And it’s not just the polls. The results of recent special elections also point to Democrats going into the midterms with momentum behind them. So, for that matter, does the long history of midterm elections going back to the dawn of party politics; they tend to favor the party out of power.

But whether Democrats can translate these enormous national advantages into control of the Senate and a significant House majority — which would give Democrats more oversight power and, in the case of the Senate, leverage over Trump’s nominations — is a more complicated question.

The George W. Bush example

Winning control of the House, where every seat will be up for election, is easier than winning control of the Senate, where only one-third of seats are up for grabs in any election year. To win the Senate, Democrats will need to win at least two seats where Trump won by at least 11 points in the last election. That’s really tough, even in a wave year.

The 2006 midterms offer a useful comparison.

As my colleague Carl Hulse recently pointed out, there are a lot of similarities between Trump’s predicament today and George W. Bush’s that year. Both presidents were unpopular: Trump’s approval rating is just 38 percent among likely voters; Bush’s was about the same. Bush was in a quagmire in Iraq and dogged by high gas prices. Today, Trump has just a 31 percent approval rating on the war in Iran and a 28 percent rating on the cost of living.

Even so, to flip the Senate in 2006, Democrats needed to win at least a few seats in states where Bush had won by at least eight points in the previous election. In the end, they pulled it off — but only barely, including two extremely narrow victories of less than one point in Montana and Virginia. Without a few fortunate breaks, those races could have gone the other way, along with the Senate. The result would have been less aggressive oversight of the Iraq war, among other differences.

The national environment may have been great for Democrats, but a Senate win was far from inevitable.

Too far to the left?

With Trump’s approval ratings so far underwater, Republicans may have only one realistic card to play: try to rally their base and hold on to Republican-leaning independents by casting the Democrats as too far to the left.

Republicans didn’t have a similar opportunity in 2006, when Democrats assiduously nominated moderate candidates in key red states and districts. While Democrats have nominated candidates with broad appeal in most states this year, there are at least a few competitive races — most notably the Senate contest in Michigan — where Democrats have nominated candidates far to the left of anything the party would have contemplated 20 years ago. They’ve also nominated left-wing candidates in a number of noncompetitive races, which has driven considerable national media coverage of the party’s lurch to the left.

The poll does contain hints that primary victories this summer by progressive and democratic socialist candidates have made the Democratic Party less palatable to some voters. About half of voters — 50 percent of likely voters — say the party is “too far” to the left. That’s up from 46 percent in the last Times/Siena poll of registered voters in May, which was conducted before the democratic socialist surge in New York, Colorado and beyond.

But it’s also hard to see any sign it’s damaging Democrats in the survey results — and in particular, in any question that pits Democrats against Republicans. Voters say, for instance, that Republicans are more extreme than Democrats by an eight-point margin, 48-40.

And at a time when Republicans hold the White House and Congress, voters will tend to be much more concerned about Republican excesses than Democratic ones. That’s part of what makes midterm elections so hard for the party in power.

item.title: British Columbia Sues OpenAI Over Tumbler Ridge Shooting
item.description:
British Columbia sued OpenAI in U.S. federal court on Monday, claiming that the company had failed to report to the police the violent comments made by a user of its chatbot who went on to kill nine people and injure two.

The shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, killed herself, the authorities said, after the Feb. 10 rampage that shook Tumbler Ridge, a mountain town of 2,400 people in rural British Columbia.

Ms. Van Rootselaar documented some of her mental health issues and curiosity about violence, firearms and illegal narcotics on social media, and had at least two ChatGPT accounts. One account was shut down in June last year, eight months before the attacks, for having violated OpenAI’s user policy, but the company did not alert the authorities to the nature of the content.

More than 30 lawsuits have been filed against OpenAI by families of the victims, including that of a 12-year-old student, Maya Gebala, who sustained a life-altering brain injury after she was shot at close range three times.

Niki Sharma, British Columbia’s attorney general, said the province was “bringing the fight to OpenAI” by pursuing litigation in California, where the company’s headquarters are, as opposed to in Canada. The move also raises the possibility of a large payout to the victims; personal injuries compensation in Canada is generally lower than in the United States.

“No company should be exempt from accountability simply because the technology is new,” Ms. Sharma told reporters at a news conference Monday afternoon.

In its lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for Northern California, the government claims that the shooting could have been stopped if the company had heeded internal claims, made by a human review team, to refer its concerns to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

But, the government alleges, leaders at OpenAI rejected this option and instead deactivated Ms. Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account, though she retained access to the platform through a different account. The lawsuit cited a report in The Wall Street Journal about OpenAI’s review process.

In April, roughly two months after the shooting, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, apologized for the company’s failure to notify law enforcement in an open letter. David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, called the apology “necessary, and yet grossly insufficient,” and urged the company to undertake reforms that would mandate law enforcement reporting.

But, in its suit, the government claims that the company has not meaningfully engaged in safety-regulation discussions in the shooting’s aftermath.

Representatives from OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Legal proceedings cannot undo the immense loss experienced by the people of Tumbler Ridge,” said Ms. Sharma. “But pursuing accountability matters, transparency matters and strengthening protections to help prevent future tragedies matters.”

The community’s school board, after consulting with families, began work to demolish the school last month. While specific amounts for the damages sought were not included in the lawsuit, Ms. Sharma said the government would possibly use funds sought to reimburse the cost of building a new school.

item.title: ​Urging Pivot on North Korea, South’s Leader Calls for Easing Sanctions
item.description:
Breaking with decades of policy on North Korea, the president of South Korea, Lee Jae Myung, is now urging the United States to ease sanctions on Pyongyang in exchange for an agreement that it freeze its weapons programs.

“I believe there is significant value in a trade-off between sanctions — which are not particularly effective anyway — and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology,” Mr. Lee said in an interview with The New York Times on Friday.

However unpalatable such a bargain may seem, the world has no realistic alternative, Mr. Lee argued. North Korea is increasingly brandishing its nuclear missiles against the South. It is no longer the isolated pariah that Washington has tried to tame through a mix of pressure and dialogue as the wars in Ukraine and Iran have altered the geopolitical landscape.

Both Russia and China have re-embraced North Korea as a strategic partner, particularly after the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, deployed troops and weapons to support Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That conflict, alongside American strikes in Iran, has only strengthened North Korea’s resolve to expand its nuclear deterrent.

Still, Mr. Lee believes that President Trump is the only leader capable of drawing Mr. Kim back to the negotiating table. South Korean officials say Mr. Trump represents the North Korean leader’s best opportunity to sign a peace treaty for the Korean War, which never formally ended, and normalize relations with Washington.

Some analysts warn it is naïve to expect the two leaders to forge a substantial deal, but Mr. Lee asked what option is left but diplomacy.

“Aiming for denuclearization under the current circumstances,” Mr. Lee warned, “guarantees that nothing will be accomplished.”

Once a freeze is secured, he envisions building trust through reciprocal incentives and concessions to eventually convince the North to reduce its nuclear arsenal. The ultimate goal would be to create an environment where Pyongyang feels secure enough to survive without nuclear weapons.

This week, Mr. Lee will visit New York, where he will present his vision for peace and coexistence on the Korean Peninsula to the United Nations.

Mr. Lee spoke with The Times for about 70 minutes at the House of Eternal Spring, a tile-roofed banquet hall nestled within the Blue House compound, the traditional seat of the South Korean presidency. His predecessor, Yoon Suk Yeol, a conservative, moved the presidential office to the Defense Ministry headquarters before declaring martial law two years ago, starting a turbulent political period that ended in his impeachment and imprisonment.

Mr. Lee’s decision to return the presidency to the Blue House upon his inauguration 15 months ago was meant to signal a return to normalcy. During a recent university graduation, he posed for selfies with students — a stark contrast to Mr. Yoon, whose bodyguards tackled and gagged a student protester two years earlier.

But Mr. Lee, 61, is facing his own problems. His approval ratings have nearly halved since April as many South Koreans blame his government for soaring home prices and a recent stock market crash​.

He also faces mounting pressure from Mr. Trump, who recently called him ungrateful for refusing to back the American war against Iran. During the interview, Mr. Lee defended his stance on Iran, saying that South Korea’s Constitution barred him from deploying troops to a war already underway between foreign countries.

The South Korean president is also seeking to defuse trade tensions with Mr. Trump. South Korean negotiators are racing to implement a deal struck between the two leaders last fall, in which Seoul agreed to invest $350 billion in the United States in exchange for lower tariffs on South Korean products.

To placate Mr. Trump, South Korea may offer to build a gas power plant in Texas and eight nuclear power plants across the United States, according to people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Lee insisted he was unfazed by Mr. Trump’s criticisms. “I fully understand that from his perspective, the U.S. president may make various remarks,” he said.

Mr. Lee hopes to leverage Mr. Trump’s enduring fascination with the North Korean dictator to convince the U.S. leader to restart stalled talks and de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

Mr. Lee hopes dialogue between North Korea and the United States would improve his own nation’s relations with its neighbor to the north, which have deteriorated in recent years. North Korea has demolished roads and railways that once linked the two Koreas while also adding minefields and other barriers along their already heavily fortified border.

By contrast, North Korea is moving closer to both Moscow and Beijing​. After supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine, the North has opened a bridge along its border with Russia and is about to open another one with China.​

The collapse of inter-Korean communication has eliminated South Korea’s ability to serve as a mediator between Mr. Kim and Mr. Trump, a role Seoul played in helping arrange three summit meetings during Mr. Trump’s first term.​ Those meetings ended without agreement on ​denuclearizing North Korea.

Backed by Russia and China and buoyed by renewed economic growth, Mr. Kim is no longer as desperate for a deal with Mr. Trump and now possesses greater leverage to demand more favorable terms​, analysts have said.​ Still, Mr. Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to revive his personal diplomacy with Mr. Kim, often boasting of their “very good relationship.”

Last month, Mr. Trump unilaterally scaled back a major annual joint military exercise with South Korea, describing it as “hostile” toward Mr. Kim. North Korea, for its part, said that Mr. Kim retained “good memories and feelings about Trump” from their previous meetings.

Mr. Lee is not alone in calling for a change in strategy to revive talks with the North. At a forum in South Korea last week​, Stephen E. Biegun, who led U.S. negotiations with North Korea during Mr. Trump’s first term, said the United States could negotiate a “slowing or freezing” of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal.​

Others are more skeptical about a breakthrough. Cheong Seong-chang, a senior analyst at the Seoul-based Sejong Institute, cautioned that Mr. Trump may be more interested in creating a diplomatic spectacle with Mr. Kim, such as a surprise visit to Pyongyang, to divert public attention from the prolonged war with Iran. Nor would achieving a lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula be Mr. Kim’s main concern, he said.

Mr. Lee says the current stalemate in relations is simply too risky to be allowed to continue, as North Korea is steadily expanding its nuclear arsenal.

“Our estimates suggest that North Korea is now capable of producing, or may already be producing, an additional 10 to 20 nuclear weapons each year,” Mr. Lee said. “Once it believes it has accumulated enough nuclear weapons and missiles to guarantee its survival, it will be tempted to export them to make money.”

“That will be a truly dangerous moment,” he said.

item.title: With Time on His Side, Xi Seeks to Extend Truce With Trump
item.description:
When China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, and President Trump meet in Washington this week, the two men will be operating on vastly different clocks.

The American president is constrained by the immediate demands of a midterm election in November and a grinding war. The Chinese leader is gearing up for a norm-shattering fourth term as head of the ruling Communist Party, that will keep him in power for another five years.

For Mr. Xi, the disparity in political realities gives him an edge in maintaining the truce that the two countries reached last year. A renewed trade fight would hit American consumers right before the election — a risk Mr. Trump can ill afford. China’s economy is struggling too, but Mr. Xi answers to no electorate, giving him the patience to prolong the détente on his terms.

“Each of Xi’s face-to-face encounters with Trump in his second term would only have reinforced Xi’s prior conviction that Trump is leading an America that is dangerous but declining,” said Jonathan Czin, a researcher at the Brookings Institution who previously worked at the C.I.A. analyzing Chinese politics.

Mr. Xi, who will sit down for talks with Mr. Trump on Thursday, may be wagering that leaning into Mr. Trump’s preference for leader-to-leader diplomacy can insulate the relationship from flash points like the status of Taiwan, the self-governed island claimed by Beijing, and the competition to dominate artificial intelligence.

Keeping Mr. Trump at bay would give Mr. Xi breathing room to work on rejuvenating his listless economy, which has been weakened by a property crisis, high youth unemployment and excess production. It would give him time to rebuild the upper echelons of his military leadership, which he has hollowed out in a drive against corruption and disloyalty. And it would allow him to continue expanding his country’s industrial, technological and military strength for a future showdown with the United States.

Analysts say China benefits every time Mr. Trump’s attention drifts elsewhere. By quarreling with traditional American allies or sinking deeper into the war in Iran, Mr. Trump is weakening his country's global standing and pulling troops away from the Pacific.

“Xi would love to tell Trump, ‘Go on, stay the course,’” said Suisheng Zhao, executive director of the China Center at the University of Denver. “For Xi, Trump represents a window of opportunity for China, so his priority is to buy more time.”

Since first meeting Mr. Trump at Mar-a-Lago more than nine years ago — a gathering best remembered for being when Mr. Xi learned about U.S. missile strikes on Syria while dining on what Mr. Trump described as the “most beautiful chocolate cake” — Mr. Xi has had an extraordinary amount of time for a Chinese leader to size up his chief geopolitical rival.

Early in Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Xi was somewhat accommodating toward the American president. In 2018, his government agreed to purchase $200 billion in additional U.S. goods and services to offset a trade imbalance (though Beijing never fully honored that deal.)

Last year, Mr. Xi flipped the dynamic between the two superpowers.

Faced with Mr. Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, Mr. Xi was the only world leader who refused to back down, choosing instead to match his opponent with one sky-high tariff after another. Mr. Xi then reached for his ace card by throttling exports of Chinese critical minerals, or rare earths, which companies globally need for modern technologies. Backed into a corner, the Trump administration called for a truce.

It was a payoff years in the making: a rare instance in which Beijing not only withstood U.S. pressure but turned the tables and forced it to relent. Beijing, as a result, is emboldened today and sees itself more as an equal to Washington, analysts say.

The Trump administration “thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions. And that did not occur. In fact, the opposite did,” said Scott Kennedy, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

“I think now this is Xi Jinping’s world and we’re all living in it,” he added.

The superpowers should put limits on competition, Mr. Xi’s argument goes, to avoid what he has warned could be a catastrophic clash. To this end, he has pushed a formula he calls “constructive strategic stability.”

In practice, what this means is that Beijing wants Washington to accept boundaries on where it can challenge China.

In July, for example, when the U.S. Federal Communications Commission proposed a ban on Chinese-made humanoid robots, China’s Ministry of Commerce invoked the phrase, demanding that Washington roll back the restrictions to preserve “strategic stability.”

American analysts view the slogan not as a serious effort at ironing out differences but as an attempt to get Washington to recognize China’s clout and back off. China could apply it to any new U.S. restrictions on chip exports or arms sales to Taiwan.

“The truce is not constructive because little diplomatic infrastructure is being built,” Mr. Czin of the Brookings Institution said. “It is tactical rather than strategic. And therefore it is inherently unstable.”

Mr. Xi appears to have calculated that the best way to manage the United States is to engage Mr. Trump in high-profile summits rich in optics but thin in substance.

The planned meeting on Thursday will be their third face-to-face in less than a year, a pace that could continue with talks in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

“Head-of-state diplomacy is the cornerstone of China-U.S. relations,” China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, told Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a call on Thursday.

But beyond extending the trade truce, the meetings have produced few breakthroughs. China may agree to more agricultural purchases this week, but expectations are low on issues like A.I. safety or China’s trade imbalances.

That is by design, analysts say. Enticing Mr. Trump with the pageantry of summits he seems to relish lowers the risk that he may do something to derail relations — like greenlight a package of arms to Taiwan.

Tellingly, Mr. Trump has avoided criticizing China in the lead-up to the talks, even downplaying a Wall Street Journal report that China had supplied Iran with satellite images of a U.S. base in Jordan where three American troops were killed in an Iranian strike.

The summitry will also serve a domestic purpose for Mr. Xi by burnishing his image at home as a global statesman, during a moment of economic anxiety for many Chinese. It is important for Mr. Xi to demonstrate that he can manage Beijing’s most critical bilateral relationship, analysts say.

Mr. Trump is expected to greet Mr. Xi personally on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland when his plane lands on Wednesday. The White House will host Mr. Xi and Peng Liyuan, the first lady, for a state dinner, the first such banquet since King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited in April.

“Xi wants to be seen by the Chinese public as a highly respected, influential and consequential world leader — and nothing can top being wined and dined at the White House,” said Minxin Pei, a professor at Claremont McKenna College who studies Chinese leadership politics.

“Xi cannot afford to be distracted by a huge confrontation with the United States,” Mr. Pei said.

Berry Wang contributed research.

item.title: Japan, Suffering Xi’s Ire, Hopes Trump Can Help Temper China
item.description:
For almost a year, China has orchestrated a bruising campaign against Japan in retaliation for a comment by its prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, in defense of Taiwan.

When Ms. Takaichi meets with President Trump in New York City on Tuesday, those tensions are likely to be high on the agenda.

Ms. Takaichi, a longtime critic of Beijing, is expected to express her concern to Mr. Trump about China’s increasingly aggressive economic and security measures, according to two people familiar with her plans, including restrictions on the export of rare earth minerals. She will also emphasize her desire for a de-escalation with China, the individuals said.

The meeting between Mr. Trump and Ms. Takaichi, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, comes a day before Mr. Trump is set to welcome China’s leader, Xi Jinping, for a state visit in Washington. Ms. Takaichi remains focused on persuading Mr. Trump to maintain security commitments in East Asia, including the more than 50,000 American troops stationed in Japan.

Kenneth R. Weinstein, Japan chair at Hudson Institute, a think tank in Washington, said that Ms. Takaichi had a strong relationship with Mr. Trump and that she would likely seek to reaffirm their alliance as a buffer against Mr. Xi.

“She wants President Trump to send a clear signal to Xi Jinping that there is no distance between the U.S. and Japan on an array of critical issues,” he said.

Ms. Takaichi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the tensions with China and her meeting with Mr. Trump.

China and Japan have been at odds since November, when Ms. Takaichi said that Japan could intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that Beijing considers part of its territory. Beijing unleashed a wave of reprisals, restricting Japanese seafood imports, discouraging tourism to Japan and limiting the export of critical minerals to Japan. Chinese officials also cut off diplomatic channels to Tokyo.

The economic pressure has intensified in recent months, with tourism from China falling sharply — the number of Chinese tourists was down 59 percent in August from the previous year — and Beijing further restricting the export of rare earth minerals used in a range of essential technologies.

China in July exported 122 tons of rare earth magnets to Japan, according to Chinese customs data, a 52 percent drop from the year before. In August, China’s rare earth magnets to Japan were 17 percent lower compared with a year earlier.

In recent months, Ms. Takaichi’s government has attempted to re-engage with China, sending delegations of lawmakers and business leaders to Beijing.

Those visits have yielded some frank conversations. During one recent meeting in Beijing, Chinese officials peppered their Japanese visitors with questions about Ms. Takaichi’s plans to build up Japan’s military, asking if she was doing so with the goal of being able to defend Taiwan, according to a Japanese lawmaker who was present. The lawmaker asked not to be named because the meeting was private.

During another recent visit, Masahiro Komura, a Japanese lawmaker who is a member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, pressed his Chinese counterparts on export restrictions and the recent detention of Japanese nationals on smuggling charges. Asked in an interview whether the talks had yielded any breakthroughs, he joked that it was a positive sign that no Japanese lawmakers were detained in China during the visit.

“The top priority is to continue the diplomatic relationship,” he said. “Without communication between two countries, both sides will become very skeptical, and a negative situation will escalate.”

Chinese officials have used the recent visits from Japanese lawmakers as an opportunity to underline their unhappiness with Ms. Takaichi. In private, they have remained fixated on Ms. Takaichi’s remark on Taiwan, according to Japanese participants in the meetings, demanding that she retract it.

China’s assistant minister of foreign affairs, Liu Bin, lectured a group of Japanese lawmakers when they met last week. He said Ms. Takaichi’s “erroneous remarks and actions” were the primary obstacle and that Japan should “demonstrate through concrete actions that it is worthy of the trust of its Asian neighbors.”

In a meeting with another Japanese delegation in late August, Lu Kang, deputy head of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Department, said that “China-Japan relations are facing serious difficulties, and the root causes are clear.”

Ms. Takaichi’s advisers say she has no intention of backing down from her remarks, given her long history of support for Taiwan and widespread anxiety about China among the Japanese public.

Ms. Takaichi and Mr. Xi are set to cross paths again in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum meeting in Shenzhen. Neither side has commented yet on whether the two leaders will set aside time to meet one on one.

Lian Degui, director of the Center for Japanese Studies at Shanghai International Studies University, said the recent meetings between Chinese and Japanese officials showed there was the potential for relations to be repaired, depending on the messages from Ms. Takaichi’s administration.

“If China finds the attitude acceptable, then Japan-China relations can move to the next phase of improvement,” Mr. Lian said. “The prerequisite for improving relations is for the Japanese government to admit its mistake.”

The lack of a trusted intermediary between the two sides is another obstacle, analysts said. Under Ms. Takaichi, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party has lost the support of the Komeito party, formerly its main coalition partner, which had served as a conduit to China.

“What is lacking,” said Chen Hong, director of the Asia Pacific Studies Centre at East China Normal University in Shanghai, “is someone who can be taken seriously by Beijing and genuinely influence Takaichi’s decision-making.”

In New York, Ms. Takaichi and Mr. Trump have a full agenda, including questions about trade, defense and Tokyo’s currency woes. Japan has watched with concern as Mr. Trump has in recent weeks pressured allies like South Korea to provide support for the war in Iran; Ms. Takaichi appears eager to avoid the same fate.

Ms. Takaichi also faces pressure at home to question Mr. Trump about his administration’s recent decision to sanction the president of the International Criminal Court, Tomoko Akane, a Japanese judge. The decision has stirred deep anger in Japan, and Ms. Takaichi has called it “very unfortunate.”

It is unclear if Mr. Trump wants to get further involved in China’s dispute with Japan, though he has previously vowed to speak “Japan’s praises” to Mr. Xi.

Mr. Weinstein, the expert, said that is unlikely that Mr. Trump would ask Mr. Xi to “dial back the pressure” on Japan.

“The best thing the president can do,” he said, “is continue to send the signal — by regularly consulting Prime Minister Takaichi — that the U.S.-Japan alliance is critical to the United States, Japan and the Indo-Pacific.”

Hisako Ueno contributed reporting from Tokyo, and Pei-Lin Wu from Taipei, Taiwan.

item.title: Trump’s U.N. Speech Comes at a Time of Tumult
item.description:
President Trump will address global leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday morning as he is confronted with a deeply unpopular war in Iran, rising concerns about the unpredictability of artificial intelligence and allies that have begun to openly question whether the United States remains a credible partner.

In addition to a series of global crises, Mr. Trump is also juggling a packed schedule. After delivering his address, the president is expected to meet with leaders of Britain, Japan, Venezuela and a number of Persian Gulf nations.

He is also expected to sign an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that Mr. Trump says will expand the U.S. security presence in the semiautonomous Danish territory, according to a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity to preview the schedule. The signing comes after Mr. Trump this year demanded total control of Greenland, a threat that prompted intense criticism from allies who will be at the opening of the United Nations session in New York.

Mr. Trump will again face a United Nations that he has long derided as outdated, inefficient and beholden to powers that revel in defying American wishes. But this year, more than most, he is increasingly isolated on the world stage. Here are some of the more pressing issues he will encounter at the 81st session of the General Assembly.

Mr. Trump enters the summit with a track record of attacking, rather than uniting, many of the attendees.

When he first attended the gathering as president in 2017, Mr. Trump was largely subdued. That was not the case last year, when he questioned whether the U.N should exist, lectured the world leaders about their immigration policies and bashed allies and foes across the globe. “Your countries are going to hell,” Mr. Trump said.

But that was before his biggest international gamble yet — starting a war with Iran that he was convinced would topple its 47-year-old leadership — went south. He makes no secret of his anger at allies who refused to help open the Strait of Hormuz and who declared that his war was illegal.

The president may be the odd man out even more so this time around. He has attacked many European leaders for not supporting the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran. His threats to take over Greenland nearly upended the Western alliance and in part prompted Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada to warn of a “rupture” in the world order. The United States and Canada are still locked in a trade war.

Mr. Trump met with France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, at Trump Tower on Monday, and it remains to be seen how Mr. Trump will approach his first meeting with Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham. But the introduction will come after Mr. Trump weighed in on a highly divisive subject this month by endorsing the unification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, which is still part of the United Kingdom. That came just days after Mr. Burnham had said reunification was off the table for now.

Mr. Trump will join members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the U.S. allies Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. The nations in the Gulf region are likely to raise concerns about the soaring energy prices caused by the fallout of the war in Iran, which has shown little sign of ending.

Mr. Trump will argue in his speech that the war in Iran is necessary to prevent the nation from having a nuclear weapon, according to a U.S. official speaking on the condition of anonymity to preview the summit. That message has not helped quell worries among Americans over the war in Iran, its disruption of supply chains and the fueling of economic anxiety.

In addition to the conflict in Iran, Mr. Trump must also decide whether he should aid the Saudis in their fight against the Iranian-backed Houthis. Mr. Trump so far has resisted the Saudi Arabia’s appeals to have the United States launch strikes in Yemen.

The threat posed by artificial intelligence has jumped to the top of the U.N. agenda, after a summer of surprises, including A.I. agents that broke out of the “sandboxes” where they were being tested, conducted cyberattacks on their own and covered their tracks. Now Mr. Trump, while dismissing potential serious threats as a “HOAX” and deflecting calls for him to impose guardrails on the new technology, is trying to figure out the value of slowing down Chinese progress, as well. He has said that efforts to rein in A.I. amount to a “sick conspiracy.”

Some officials in the Trump administration are urging caution in embracing artificial intelligence, particularly after some A.I. agents went rogue. But Mr. Trump’s anti-regulatory stance is also fueled by influential Silicon Valley voices like David Sacks, the venture capitalist who interceded to weaken an executive order in May that would have required safety reviews of new A.I. models; Mark Zuckerberg of Meta; and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

Mr. Trump will have his first in-person meeting with Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s new leader after the United States deposed and captured Nicolás Maduro, who is imprisoned just across the East River in Brooklyn.

Ms. Rodríguez has gained favor with Mr. Trump since the military operation, particularly by allowing the United States to expand its access and control over Venezuela’s oil reserves. Mr. Trump last month announced a deal to take majority control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves, as he hopes to assert dominance over energy in the Western Hemisphere.

item.title: Italy’s Prisons Were Overcrowded. Then They Overheated.
item.description:
As Italy sweltered through its hottest summer in 75 years, inmates at one of the country’s largest prisons took to sleeping on their cell floors, according to Fabio Falbo, one of those incarcerated there.

Despite the cockroaches scuttling across the concrete, the ground was cooler than their bunks, Mr. Falbo explained to me in a letter from the Rebibbia prison in Rome.

All told, it was the worst summer in his 17 years of incarceration, a “claustrophobic hell of stone and flesh,” wrote Mr. Falbo, who is serving a murder sentence, though he maintains his innocence.

Across Italy’s roughly 200 detention facilities this summer, record heat levels made the penal experience a health hazard as well as a punishment, according to interviews with prisoners, jailers, prison directors and rights campaigners.

Temperatures inside cells regularly topped 100 degrees Fahrenheit, according to an independent prison watchdog, Antigone. That heat — coupled with the absence of air-conditioning, a shortage of fans and inadequate ventilation — placed “a significant strain on correctional facilities, exacerbating pre-existing logistical problems,” the watchdog said in a recent report.

The stifling conditions are compounded by widespread overcrowding, a problem that successive governments have failed to solve. There are nearly 65,000 prisoners in Italian detention facilities, crammed into cells built for less than 47,000.

The situation is tough even for prison guards. After temperatures hit 120 degrees Fahrenheit in a jail in Puglia, southern Italy, a guards’ union filed a complaint with prosecutors. “Prison guards are a mirror of what happens inside the prison,” said Fabrizio Lofoco, a lawyer for the guards.

The heat makes the overcrowded prisons even harder to manage, said Vito Ferrara, a guard in southern Italy. This summer, it was “commonplace” for inmates to feel unwell or to act out aggressively, Mr. Ferrara said. “We go into the trenches every day, we cross ourselves, and then we don’t know how it’s going to end,” he added.

The Justice Ministry declined to comment on the accounts in this article.

The ministry instead referred me to July news reports quoting Stefano Carmine De Michele, head of the prison administration department, who said that his office had allocated roughly $920,000 to pay for refrigerators and fans. Air-conditioning in the cells? “It’s not being considered,” he said at that time.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government has pledged to build more prisons and recently passed a law that could allow some drug addicts to serve their sentences in treatment centers or at home.

That has yet to reduce the prison population. And the government, which has a tough-on-crime agenda, has also introduced dozens of criminal offenses, lengthened prison terms and restricted other sentence reductions.

Prison wardens say their hands are tied by financial restraints and aging structures. Some prisons are more than 100 years old, while Antigone found that some 40 percent were built between 1980 and 1999, before heat became such a problem.

Claudia Clementi, the warden at Regina Coeli, a 17th-century convent in Rome that was retrofitted as a prison in the 19th century, said that installing air-conditioning in the cells there would be technically difficult.

Speaking in her air-conditioned office in another section of the prison, Ms. Clementi said the real problem was overcrowding. Among other things, overcrowding made it hard to provide enough shower time for every inmate, she said. It was also difficult to staff enough rehabilitation programs that “keep people occupied and mitigate some of the hardest aspects” of incarceration, she added.

She noted that the prison’s thick stone walls and high ceilings helped to create “a microclimate” that made it “a little better than other places.” The prison’s chaplain, the Rev. Vittorio Trani, said that might be true in the morning, when the walls absorbed some heat, but in the afternoon, “it gets really bad because the heat is released like a radiator.”

In July, campaigners gathered outside Regina Coeli to highlight the conditions as temperatures hovered around 100 degrees Fahrenheit outside. The prison held more than 1,000 inmates, nearly double what the building was meant to hold, Ms. Clementi said.

Most of the prisoners do not have fans, said Stefano Anastasia, a former regional ombudsman for detainees. And like most prisoners in Italy, the inmates at Regina Coeli are kept inside their cells for most of the day. One of the few opportunities for outside activity, Ms. Clementi said, was from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m., when more staff members were on duty.

“You can imagine what the sun feels like at that time,” Mr. Anastasia said.

As a result, according to the Antigone report, many inmates often preferred to stay in their overheated rooms, “increasing the time spent in cramped spaces.”

In the Rebibbia prison, the cramped cells have narrow windows that trap air, “sealing in the mugginess,” Mr. Falbo wrote in his letter.

He has a fan in his cell, but this summer it provided little relief, added Mr. Falbo, who writes about prisoners’ rights issues under the name “the Scribe of Rebibbia” on social media.

The fan just moved hot air, he wrote, like “the draft of an industrial oven.”
