item.title: German Leaders Prepare to Deny Far Right Access to Secret War Plan
item.description:
Spooked by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the German military drafted a 1,000-page blueprint in 2024 to set out how to respond to another Russian attack in Eastern Europe. Senior leaders in Germany’s 16 states are among the few government officials allowed access to the classified document, known informally as an “Oplan.”

Now, Germany’s federal government, under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is preparing to restrict that access, in order to prevent a far-right, Moscow-friendly party — which won a recent election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt — from reviewing the plan.

That party, Alternative for Germany, or AfD, is trying to form a coalition government to take power in Saxony-Anhalt this fall. If the AfD succeeds, military leaders fear, the party might pass the plan to Russia, according to three senior officials familiar with the discussions.

The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive statecraft, as did 14 others who detailed further efforts to restrict an AfD-led state government from reviewing state secrets or blocking government cooperation.

Asked for comment, a spokesman for the German defense ministry said it was assessing what security-related information needed protection, but declined to offer further details.

A spokesman for the AfD, Jork Herrmann, said, “It would be utterly undemocratic and impossible to justify to voters to withhold intelligence information from the party based on unsubstantiated and unprovable allegations.”

The plans would affect the balance of Germany’s federalist system, which was designed after World War II to pool power between the central and state governments and grant a degree of autonomy to Germany’s regions. Under that system, each German state run its own intelligence office. The offices receive a wide range of information from federal intelligence.

Other proposals include:

Blocking Saxony-Anhalt’s ability to see intelligence concerning Russian subterfuge in Europe, while still allowing it to view other intelligence needed to thwart terrorist attacks.

Changing rules governing interstate cooperation, which currently require unanimity between the 16 state governments, to prevent AfD officials in Saxony-Anhalt from paralyzing policing programs that cross state lines.

Preventing the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, which is under federal surveillance, from viewing intelligence files related to the party and investigations into far-right extremists.

The plans sharpen a dispute among Germans about how best to protect their postwar democratic system, which was intended after the defeat of Nazism to make it harder for extremist groups to ever take power again.

Officials in Mr. Merz’s national government, a coalition led by his conservative Christian Democratic party, want to limit the AfD’s access to sensitive information because they view it as an extremist group. It is also an effort to reassure Germany’s allies, who have expressed deep concerns to Berlin over the AfD’s coziness with Moscow.

The moves could draw a court challenge from the AfD, which has complained that the country’s mainstream parties are seeking to undermine democracy by thwarting the will of voters and restricting its power in office.

German officials say it is necessary to act because of the AfD’s affinity for Russia. The AfD’s national leaders have expressed open admiration for Vladimir V. Putin, Russia’s authoritarian leader, as well as playing down the Holocaust and resurfacing Nazi slogans.

The German federal intelligence agency has designated the national AfD party as “suspected extremist” and its local chapter in Saxony-Anhalt as “confirmed extremist.” It has accused the party of promoting a racist and unconstitutional vision of nationhood that essentially relegates minorities to second-class status. The party denies it is extremist, saying the accusation is politically motivated.

Federal concerns took on new urgency when the AfD won 44 percent of the vote in state elections earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt, allowing it to begin negotiations with rivals to form a government there.

Because many AfD officials, including some of its top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, maintain strong ties with Moscow, German leaders believe it is a near-certainty that the AfD would pass intelligence related to Russian threats and the war in Ukraine back to the Kremlin.

Before the election, the German defense minister, Boris Pistorius, told one newspaper, Bild, that he would not share military intelligence with an AfD government. “Their affinity for Putin is impossible to overlook,” said Mr. Pistorius, a leader of the center-left Social Democrats, Mr. Merz’s governing partners.

Tensions between Moscow and Berlin are escalating as the war drags on and Germany continues to back Ukraine, militarily and diplomatically. German leaders have publicly blamed Russia for cyberattacks, sabotage campaigns and a recent effort to bomb cargo planes at the Leipzig airport. Russia denies the accusations.

Germany’s top military allies, including Poland and some Scandinavian countries, have expressed concern to German officials over continuing to share Russia-related information with Germany if it could be passed by an AfD state government to Moscow, five officials said.

Those officials said that Germany had assured its allies that it is preparing measures to deny Saxony-Anhalt officials access to certain sensitive intelligence in the event the AfD takes power there. The Germans have not specified exactly which intelligence they will no longer share with the state should the AfD take power, the officials said, but they said the German assurances had been convincing.

The federal government does not plan a blanket ban on intelligence sharing with Saxony-Anhalt, which could hamstring the state government’s ability to deter terrorist attacks or other calamities, six officials said.

Instead, it is planning to sever state access to certain types of intelligence, like information involving far-right groups or Russia — either for Saxony-Anhalt specifically or, in order to comply with the German Constitution, for all states.

German officials have also discussed denying an AfD government access to information about the AfD itself.

The Saxony-Anhalt wing of the AfD is under surveillance by federal intelligence, including undercover agents, because of its “confirmed extremist” designation. The AfD could use routine intelligence sharing to find those agents and otherwise thwart efforts to monitor it, German officials say.

European nations have a recent track record of restricting intelligence sharing with far-right parties.

In Austria in 2017, the far-right Freedom Party shared power as a junior partner in the federal government. The party’s current leader, Herbert Kickl, was appointed to head the interior ministry, the cabinet post that traditionally oversees domestic intelligence gathering.

Austria’s allies, including the United States, worried that his control of the ministry would allow far-right extremists to gain access to active intelligence investigations targeting them. Some countries began restricting the intelligence they shared with the Austrians, amid fears that it might otherwise find its way to Russia.

The mistrust reached a peak when the police raided Austria’s primary intelligence agency in 2019. A subsequent government dissolved the agency altogether in 2021 and rebuilt it from scratch.

item.title: ‘My Husband Is in Love With His Valet’: Takeaways From Charles Spencer’s Memoir
item.description:
“Swan Song” weaves Charles Spencer’s early memories of Princess Diana with the planning and execution of her funeral service. In the introduction, Spencer says that “the aim of the book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective,” just as he did during her fiery eulogy. With the 30th anniversary of her death looming, he writes, “I thought, You know what? … I am going to tell things how I remember them, lay them down for good, once and for all.”

Spencer, younger than Diana by three years, tells many affecting tales of his sister’s bravery. The one that stands out is the day the two of them, along with their mother, were checking their lobster pots off the coast of Scotland when one of them yielded a nasty surprise: a “lithe, black, muscular conger eel, which was around four feet long and as thick as my arm,” Spencer writes. As it thrashed about their boat, gnashing its sharp teeth, he and his mother cowered while Diana grabbed a penknife “and brought its point down hard behind the eel’s eyes.” (Spencer considered telling this story at Diana’s funeral but thought better of it.)

Spencer writes that Diana, who was 7 when their parents divorced, discovered that their father had married Raine, the former Countess of Dartmouth — whom the children all detested — by reading an article in the newspaper. “Diana was so disappointed and outraged by my father’s secret marriage that she slapped him across the face — the only time she physically clashed with either parent,” Spencer writes, “while saying, on behalf of Sarah, Jane and me, ‘That’s for the pain you’re causing us all.’”

Not long after she began dating Prince Charles, Diana, 19, showed up at Eton — as she often did — to take her little brother to lunch. Spencer writes that he caught sight of her red Mini Metro from his window with “a dozen strange cars and a motorbike in tow. … Diana parked carefully outside my house, while the strangers’ vehicles slewed to a halt haphazardly in the middle of the street, their ignitions still on, disgorging men — some alone, others in pairs — who converged on her like hyenas closing in on a gazelle.”

According to Spencer, shortly after their engagement, Prince Charles squeezed Diana’s waist and said, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?” Spencer also writes that he learned from a friend of Diana’s that, the day before their wedding, Prince Charles told her “that she needed to know that he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her.” Later, Spencer writes, he was visiting his sister at Kensington Palace when the thump of her disco music led Prince Charles to scream, “Get her to turn off that infernal racket!”

When Spencer’s father, the Earl of Spencer, died in 1992, Prince Charles came to Althorp with Diana for the funeral. According to Spencer, the prince said to him, “You’re just so lucky — you know, inheriting when you’re so young!” He added, “I’m 43, and I employ 50 people … but my parents insist on treating me like — like a child!”

During a tea at Althorp, the Spencers’ ancestral family home, their stepmother Raine was rude to their mother, Frances Shand Kydd. “When Diana discovered this, she confronted Raine with incredulity. … ‘Do you really have no idea how to behave?’” Raine shot back, “I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you.” Spencer writes that “Diana paused for a second, surprised at the intensity of the spite. She then took a step forward, hooked a long leg round Raine’s calves before shoving her down the carpeted staircase.”

Spencer writes that over lunch at her favorite London restaurant, Diana told him, “I’m going to get divorced,” adding, “My husband is in love with his valet.” Diana, Spencer says, “did not name the member of staff, and I never asked her who it was, or why she would believe such an improbable thing. It was not important: The end of her marriage, and of her dreams, was.”

Spencer is frank about the ups and downs of his relationship with his sister. “The astonishing pressures of her life, and her reactive nature, saw her fall out with each of us regularly,” Spencer writes. “She was on non-speaks with two of our closest relatives for months before her death, over not very much at all.”

When Spencer learned that the palace had extended funeral invitations to Fleet Street editors, he placed calls to all of them, asking them to stay home. “They were unable to be rude to the brother of the much-mourned princess and, although clearly highly surprised by my call, they each agreed not to come,” Spencer writes. “The only one who sounded surly, as opposed to merely confused or embarrassed, was Piers Morgan of The Mirror, who snarled with annoyance before he hung up.”

At the rehearsal the day before the funeral, Spencer realized with a start that he had, in effect, walked into an ambush, that the assembled courtiers were there to vet his eulogy. Bluffing his way out of the situation, he told them: “God, I’m stupid! … In all the excitement of getting here on time, I’ve only gone and left my speech at home!”

When Diana’s service at Westminster Abbey concluded, Spencer writes, he got on the royal train headed back to Althorp for her burial, where his brother-in-law Robert Fellowes — Queen Elizabeth’s private secretary — told him that the monarch, who had stripped Diana of her royal titles after the divorce, had offered to reinstate them. Spencer replied: “That’s very kind of the queen, of course. But what’s the point, Robert? Now? I mean — Diana’s dead.”

item.title: A Missile of a Memoir as Diana’s Brother Takes Aim at British Royals
item.description:
In 1997, Earl Spencer, the 33-year-old head of one of Britain’s most distinguished aristocratic dynasties, stood before the world and delivered a stirring public rebuke to the British royal family. The occasion was the funeral of his sister Diana, the Princess of Wales, whose death in a car accident in Paris had unleashed a torrent of grief from a nation long accustomed to concealing its feelings.

At one point, the earl angrily alluded to Buckingham Palace’s decision to strike “Her Royal Highness” from Diana’s name as a condition of her divorce from Prince Charles, the future king of England, a year earlier. His sister, he said pointedly, “proved in the last year that she needed no royal title to continue to generate her particular brand of magic.”

No one who witnessed the earl’s extraordinary oration, which drew spontaneous applause from spectators watching on screens outside, will ever forget the shock of it, even at a funeral full of shocking details. (For starters, Queen Elizabeth, who was seated impassively in the church and was by default one of the objects of his remarks, was the earl’s godmother; Robert Fellowes, the Queen’s private secretary, was his brother-in-law, married to his sister Jane.)

And now, nearly 30 years later, comes an even more startling addition to the record of that dizzying, bewildering time. On Tuesday, Earl Spencer, now 62, is publishing “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” a memoir of his and Diana’s connected lives that, among other things, revisits the days surrounding her death. And if he seemed angry at the royal family 29 years ago — and angrily determined to stand up for his own family in the face of what he saw as heavy-handed callousness by theirs — it is clear now that the public didn’t know the half of it.

Though Diana and Charles proved to be singularly ill-suited for each other, it wasn’t because they came from different worlds. Their families had been intertwined for years. And so the events the earl describes in his new book are from the perspective of someone who feels his family — which can trace its history back to the 15th century, and which has occupied its family seat, Althorp, for more than 500 years — is if not exactly equal to, than at least as formidable as the royal family.

The events he’s describing are nearly three decades old, and impossible to prove one way or the other. In the ensuing years, Earl Spencer, who uses his given name, Charles Spencer, professionally, has worked as a journalist, historian and podcast host and written nine nonfiction books, including “A Very Private School,” an account of the monstrous abuse he and other boys suffered at Maidwell, a boarding school he began attending at the age of 8.

Divorced from his first three wives, he married for the fourth time earlier this year.

The most incendiary news in “Swan Song” comes when Earl Spencer describes the telephone conversations he says he had with Prince Charles after Diana’s death. They read like grenades lobbed lazily over a fence and intended to destroy everything in a neighbor’s yard.

At first, Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time,” the earl says. Perhaps, he writes, the prince was thinking about “now being free to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not” — a reference to the prince’s longtime companion, Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla.

Worse was to come when the two argued over the funeral arrangements. Though the royal family had effectively excommunicated Diana after the divorce, the earl writes, it “felt entitled to take the lead” in planning the event; the Spencers “were simply expected to fall in line.”

He says that when Prince Charles learned that he objected to the plan cooked up by the royal family to have Princes Harry and William, then 12 and 15, walk behind their mother’s coffin as it approached Westminster Abbey, Charles telephoned him in a rage.

His temper worsened when the earl, the princes’ uncle, said that Diana wouldn’t have wanted her sons to undergo such an ordeal.

“That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty!” Earl Spencer says Charles — whom he describes as a “bellowing buffoon” — told him. (At this point, the earl says, he thought of “all the generations of Spencers, in their gilded frames at Althorp, who had served King, Queen and Country dutifully, as ambassadors, admirals, courtiers, politicians and viceroys.”)

At the end of his outburst, Charles turned his attention back to Diana, the book says. “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed,” Earl Spencer writes. “‘We’ll forget her soon enough!’” The earl hung up the phone after that, he says.

King Charles did not directly deny the account, but his office released a statement that was a denial of sorts.

“His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss.”

In response, Earl Spencer reiterated his recollection of the events — “those are exactly the words he said,” he told the BBC — and declared that “it is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the King.”

The world is awash in royal gossip and descriptions of who said what to whom in private conversations. But most of these are second- and thirdhand. It’s rare to hear from one of the principals, and rarer still to hear it in the form of a book this candid. The only modern precedent for Earl Spencer’s book is Prince Harry’s 2023 memoir, “Spare,” a raw burst of unprocessed pain and anger directed in large part at Prince William and King Charles for the way Harry believes they treated him and his wife, the former Meghan Markle.

Much of the criticism of “Swan Song” so far in the U.K. has focused on the potential damage the new book — whether accurate or not — might do to King Charles, currently dealing with his own health problems, as well as the disgrace of his younger brother Andrew and the unhelpful (for him) return of Harry and Meghan to England after their self-imposed exile in California.

“To the King’s supporters it is an act of revenge served so cold it comes with a layer of permafrost,” Rebecca English wrote in The Daily Mail. “While there has been little love lost between the House of Windsor and the Spencers over the decades, few predicted a hatchet-job of such deliberate spite.”

But Richard Kay, a longtime royal reporter for The Mail and a close confidant of Diana, wrote in the paper that the earl’s account matches, at least in spirit, what he told Mr. Kay on the telephone in the week after Diana’s death. According to Mr. Kay, Earl Spencer told him that he and Charles had had a “furious row” over the boys, and that Charles had been “utterly pathetic.”

Why now? In his introduction, Earl Spencer says that with the 30th anniversary of his sister’s death a year away, he has been asked numerous times to participate in documentaries about her but that he wanted to tell his story himself. He also wanted to put it behind him, he said.

“This is my final take on the situation,” he told the BBC.

item.title: A Brotherly Tribute to the People’s Princess, No Holds Barred
item.description:
SWAN SONG: Diana, My Sister, by Charles Spencer

Delivering a eulogy is hard enough. Now imagine delivering one to around 2.5 billion people.

This was the surreal task that fell to Charles Spencer, younger brother of Diana, the Princess of Walesafter she died following a car crash at 36 in the summer of 1997. Her driver, who had been trying to evade paparazzi, died at the scene, along with her boyfriend, Dodi Fayed.

In a speech that was beamed from Westminster Abbey, Spencer chastised the press whose pursuit led to Diana’s demise and sideswiped the royal family that had, among other indignities, stripped her of her title. “A girl given the name of the ancient goddess of hunting,” he noted, “was, in the end, the most hunted person of the modern age.”

The applause that followed began outside, among the hoi polloi whose adoration led to her anointment as the People’s Princess. Scattered at first, the clapping began to spread, becoming a wall of sound that rolled into the abbey, up to the vaulted ceilings, and through living rooms around the world.

Now, almost 30 years later, comes the coda: Spencer’s elegant and reproving new memoir, “Swan Song.” In between, with a degree in history from Oxford, he became a part-time journalist and wrote nine books of nonfiction, as if to model a standard of truth-telling disregarded in the “coverage” of his sister.

Save to your reading list:

Neither of Spencer’s parents lived past 70, and at 62 he feels a sense of if-not-now-when. “This is the work that really matters to me,” he writes.

The title alludes not only to his own fatalism, but to Diana’s favorite black swans from a board game that they played as children. A lament of them now circle the island where she is buried.

“Swan Song” is most compelling as a postcard from the siblings’ nursery, where their bond was solidified after their parents’ marriage dissolved in the late 1960s. (Two older sisters, Sarah and Jane, had already left the house.) He called her “Duch.” She called him “Carlos.” He still remembers “the squeak of our descent” as they slid, against the house rules, down the well-polished wooden banister of Park House.

Theirs was an upbringing typical of upper-class families, of well-appointed neglect. There were good nannies and very bad nannies, one of whom bashed their heads together or against a concrete wall. Spencer wrote about further abuse in his 2024 memoir, “A Very Private School” (as used to be customary for his class, he was sent off, miserable, at the age of 8). But contrary to reports, he writes, his father, John, the eighth Earl of Spencer, was a gentle if traditional and parsimonious soul: hiring a camel named Bert for Diana’s 7th birthday party and taking them for ice-cream outings on Brancaster beach.

Their parents’ marriage was frayed inexorably by the death of their first son, born with a hole in the back of his head and other malformations, possibly due to a Thalidomide-like medication. The children’s mother, Frances, left John for Peter Shand Kydd after falling in love with him on a ski trip, leaving Diana, who supposed herself a disappointing third daughter, permanently bereft and taking on a maternal role herself, drawing curtains against the dark at night and checking up on her “Carlos” in nursery school.

Contrary to the shy lip-biter portrayed on “The Crown,” Diana is in Spencer’s telling fierce and athletic, diving off a high slide into the family’s pool and once pushing their loathed stepmother, Raine, down a carpeted staircase like a character in “Dynasty.” On one lobster-potting trip, as others cowered, Diana killed a four-foot-long conger eel with a swift penknife blow behind the eyes.

With his pen, her brother likewise delivers a series of lacerations to his former in-laws. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, exiled from the princehood after his association with the sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein, is spotted smirking as a teen after a priest refers to “the Virgin’s womb.” Princess Anne comes off as just rude, batting away his teenage attempts at small talk. Prince Charles gets mingy when Diana tries to give her brother some unused household items bearing their shared name, then later angles to be at the center of his ex-wife’s two-mile funeral procession. (He did not prevail.) “Rest assured,” he hisses to Spencer during their discussion of funeral arrangements. “We’ll forget her soon enough.”

Yeah … no.

Even with all its bitterness toward bad actors, like the deceptive Diana interviewer Martin Bashir, this is a lyrical book that delights in moments of the British absurd. One member of Prince Charles’s retinue bleats “I am a tree!,” Monty Pythonishly, as he tries to blend in during Diana’s burial. Elsewhere, Spencer seems to relish in the chambermaids’ helplessly evocative names — Violet Collison? — and remembers thinking his mother was declaring herself “going potty,” as in crazy, when in fact she was just announcing a visit to the loo.

This is the work of a man who is resigned but has not given up.

SWAN SONG: Diana, My Sister | By Charles Spencer | Penguin Press | 384 pp. | $35

item.title: Why a Law to Help Prisoners Became a New Sectarian Flashpoint in Lebanon
item.description:
When President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon signed an amnesty law this month to free some inmates and reduce sentences for others, it was meant to ease prison overcrowding and relieve an overwhelmed judicial system.

Instead, the law has exposed and deepened political divisions in Lebanon, which has long been mired in political and economic crises and sectarianism.

In a country divided among Christian, Muslim and Druse communities, the legislation became a balancing act between competing interests, with various groups questioning accommodations made for others. Few are satisfied by the result.

Lebanon’s Constitutional Council, the highest authority in disputes about laws, suspended the law this month after some lawmakers filed an appeal challenging it. Prisoners protested the suspension, with some launching a hunger strike. The Council is expected to issue a final decision by early October.

Here’s what to know about the law and what some hoped to gain from it.

The new law was intended to deal with packed prisons and an overstretched judiciary, with many held for years without trial. It is unclear how many of them would be eligible for release under the new law.

Many prisoners have serious health problems and receive inadequate medical care, and some have died awaiting trial, according to Mahmoud Abdalla, a member of the Committee of the Families of Prisoners in Lebanon, a nonprofit advocating for the humane treatment of inmates.

Mohamed Beiruti, from the northern city of Tripoli, said his son has been incarcerated for years on suspicions of belonging to a terrorist group, without being charged and with limited access to a lawyer. “They took away every right from him,” said Mr. Beiruti, who said the accusations against his son were unfounded.

The law combines a broad amnesty for some prisoners with sentence reductions for others.

It replaces the death penalty with 28 years in prison, and life imprisonment with hard labor and a sentence of 17 years. It also reduces other sentences by a third, with special provisions for intentional or premeditated murder committed under certain aggravating circumstances.

The law excludes offenses including human trafficking, terrorist financing and repeat drug offenses.

It also excludes amnesty for Lebanese who collaborated with and fled to Israel — considered treason in Lebanon — after the Israeli military withdrew from the south of the country in 2000, following almost 20 years of occupation. However, the amnesty covers Lebanese who also fled to Israel but who did not serve in a military or security capacity.

The law was championed by Sunni Muslim lawmakers seeking to free Islamist detainees, many of them Sunni, who fought the Lebanese military over a decade ago. The lawmakers argued that the detainees had been unfairly convicted by military courts that were biased against Sunnis, at a time when Hezbollah, the Shiite Muslim militia, and its allies wielded greater influence in Lebanon.

“We needed a new page,” said Mohammad Sablouh, a human rights lawyer who has represented dozens of Sunni Islamist prisoners. Lebanon was for years, he said, “a country of gangs, not laws,” hence the need for “a national general amnesty law.”

Lebanon’s military opposed the law over concerns that it could free or reduce the sentences of people convicted of killing soldiers, according to Lebanon’s defense minister, Michel Menassa.

For the Shiite community, the priority was amnesty for Shiites detained in drug-related cases, especially smallholder cannabis farmers in the northeastern Baalbek-Hermel region. Supporters of the law said widespread poverty in the area had left residents with few options but to grow the crop.

Hussein Hajj Hassan, a lawmaker representing Hezbollah, said the effort to relieve pressure on prisons had turned into a political fight. “Unfortunately, like everything in Lebanon, it is politicized, sectarianized and ideologized,” he said.

For Lebanon’s Christian community, the aim was to provide legal relief to Lebanese who fled to Israel after its military withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000. Some were members or supporters of the South Lebanon Army, a militia that worked with Israel during the occupation.

Tony Abu Jamra, a Christian, left Lebanon for Mexico through Israel after the Israeli occupation, saying he and many others fled for fear of being branded traitors despite having no ties to Israel. He returned to his hometown, Marjayoun, in southern Lebanon, in 2006.

“Families are divided and separated,” said Mr. Abu Jamra, who works in logistics with the United Nations. “Why does someone who is not a criminal need forgiveness?”

Legal rights groups and some lawmakers argued the law should have included more explicit safeguards, such as excluding anyone who had served in the Israeli Army or committed war crimes in Lebanon, or requiring those who acquired Israeli citizenship to renounce it.

Some lawmakers also said the legislation had not been properly debated before a final vote. Others questioned whether it extended amnesty and sentence reductions beyond its intended beneficiaries.

Some lawmakers and legal rights groups even alleged that some wording in the bill had been altered by some lawmakers before it was sent to Mr. Aoun to sign.

Nizar Saghieh, co-founder of the Beirut-based advocacy group Legal Agenda, which monitors parliamentary proceedings, said the bill was changed after Parliament had voted, including modifications that removed or narrowed exclusions for certain corruption offenses. The changes come amid a broader fight over accountability for Lebanon’s 2019 banking collapse and lost deposits.

Lawmakers challenging the law before the Constitutional Council also said the text had been altered. These changes were “made in the dark,” Mr. Saghieh said. “This is destroying the rule of law.”

Mr. Aoun’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Paula Yacoubian, a lawmaker, said the signed law was “falsified” and could let major drug traffickers and corrupt officials go free.

“It’s disgraceful,” she said.

item.title: Police Officer Is Critically Wounded in Shooting Near Ontario Synagogue
item.description:
A man with a shotgun shot and critically wounded a police officer stationed outside a synagogue in Ontario on Sunday, the Canadian authorities said, as congregants gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

The officer managed to return fire, and another officer also discharged a gun, Kristy Denette, a spokeswoman with the Special Investigations Unit, the province’s police watchdog, told reporters on Monday. The first officer, identified as Constable Jeff Smith, was in stable condition, Ms. Denette said.

The suspect sustained life-threatening injuries, and some homes and vehicles in the area were hit by bullets, Ms. Denette said. The police identified the gunman as Sean Ward, 29.

The authorities did not provide information about a possible motive for the shooting, which took place near the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, a city of about 60,000 people and about a two-hour drive northeast of Toronto.

The Belleville Police Service said that an officer “encountered an individual” in the area about 7:10 p.m. Neil Ellis, the mayor of Belleville, said it was unclear whether the synagogue had been targeted.

By The New York Times

About 25 people were inside the synagogue at the time of the shooting, but no one there was injured, Mr. Ellis said.

Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks commended the injured officer’s bravery at a news conference on Monday and said uniformed patrols would be increased in the area. The Toronto Police Service said it also would increase patrols around synagogues and other places of worship, although it said there was no other known threat.

The shooting occurred at the start of Yom Kippur, a solemn day of repentance, fasting and praying. The synagogue said on social media that an episode had occurred while a service was underway on Sunday. All remaining Yom Kippur services were canceled, it added.

Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, said on social media that he was “disgusted” by the shooting. “My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear,” he said. “I expect that all those responsible are arrested and prosecuted to the full extent of the law.”

The shooting came amid heightened concerns about antisemitism and attacks on Jewish institutions in the United States, Canada and Europe.

In March, gunfire damaged three Toronto-area synagogues in less than a week, the authorities said. No one was injured.

In the same month, a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township, Mich., before killing himself during a gunfight with security guards. And an explosion damaged a synagogue in Liège, Belgium, in what the country’s interior minister called “an antisemitic act.”

In New York City in January, a man was charged with hate crimes after having repeatedly rammed his vehicle into the headquarters of Chabad-Lubavitch, a Hasidic Jewish movement. He pleaded guilty to a federal charge of intentionally damaging religious property.

On Yom Kippur last year, an attacker in Manchester, England, rammed a car into people outside a synagogue and then attacked worshipers with a knife. Two people were killed during the attack, which the police called an act of terrorism.

Vjosa Isai contributed reporting from Toronto.

item.title: One Issue That Could Upend Fragile U.S.-China Ties: Taiwan Arms
item.description:
For China’s leader, Xi Jinping, one important goal of his meeting with President Trump this week may be persuading him to keep delaying $14 billion in proposed U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

China has long claimed the self-governed island of Taiwan as its territory, and Taipei has relied on American military power to counter military threats from Beijing. When they last met, Mr. Xi warned Mr. Trump that mishandling tensions over Taiwan could be “extremely dangerous” for the United States and China, a reminder of the risk of crisis between two nuclear-armed powers.

“There’s only one issue that could cause relations between both sides to break down completely or erupt in conflict, and that is Taiwan,” said Xin Qiang, the director of the Center for Taiwan Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai.

“Demanding a continued delay in any arms sales may be the most critical issue,” he said.

Mr. Trump has described the arms sale plan as a source of leverage with China. After his May summit with Mr. Xi in Beijing, Mr. Trump said he had discussed the deal with the Chinese leader. “It’s a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly,” he said then.

Mr. Trump has since held off approving the package of missiles, anti-drone weaponry and air-defense systems. His administration has also muted public references to Taiwan: Officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have conspicuously avoided mentioning Taiwan in speeches.

For Beijing, Mr. Trump’s willingness to delay arms sales is already a gain. In Washington, Mr. Xi could hint at potential costs if Mr. Trump approves the sale, including more restrictions on Chinese rare earth exports. Mr. Xi could also signal that he might skip the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, which Mr. Trump will preside over.

Mr. Trump, for his part, may want China to increase pressure on Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for global oil and gas supplies that Iran has effectively blocked since the war began in February.

“I think in Beijing we saw the opening move in what will be a sophisticated play to get the Trump administration to reduce support for Taiwan,” said David Sacks, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who studies U.S. relations with Taiwan and China. “Xi will use his meetings with Trump in Washington to continue to implement this strategy.”

Delayed arms sales are a political headache for Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te. He has promoted increased military spending and purchases of American weapons, in part to meet the Trump administration’s own demands that partners invest more in their defense. Mr. Trump’s stalling could make it harder for Mr. Lai to defend his agenda.

Longer delays could drag on the island’s military goals, partly by pushing Taiwan further back in the line for orders of scarce military hardware, some experts said.

“Ultimately, it’s a game of the Chinese trying to prolong this process as long as possible, with the idea being that if China can make gains faster than Taiwan can acquire capabilities, then the balance continues to tilt in Beijing’s favor,” said Ryan Hass, a former director for China at the National Security Council and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

Some experts said they expected Mr. Trump to keep holding off approval of any arms sales for Taiwan until at least late this year. Others said the green light for some weapons could come sooner. Both Republicans and Democrats in Congress are likely to raise pressure on the administration to approve the proposed arms sales after the summit, Mr. Sacks said.

The arms issue has highlighted Taiwan’s struggles to keep Mr. Trump onside. Taiwan does not have formal diplomatic relations with the United States, and Mr. Trump’s highly personalized, freewheeling style makes it more difficult for Taiwan to understand and shape U.S. decision-making, experts say.

“With an administration that is so top-down, I think that is hindering the Taiwanese ability to get a really good sense of what’s going on and the ability to help shape and influence that,” said Laura Rosenberger, a former Biden administration official who oversaw U.S. policies on China and Taiwan.

In his first term, Mr. Trump signed off on about $18 billion of arms sales to Taiwan, and hawkish members of his government focused on Beijing as a long-term threat. But in his second term, Mr. Trump has emphasized pragmatic ties with China, largely retreating from a trade war after Beijing strangled exports of rare earths that are crucial for smartphones and advanced technology.

Taiwan has sought to maintain influence by cultivating Mr. Trump’s inner circle, hiring lobbyists and arranging visits to the island for prominent supporters of the president.

But some Taiwanese officials who have traveled to the United States have also been told by Trump administration officials to curtail their visits to research groups in Washington, said Mr. Hass at the Brookings Institution.

“All of this just betrays a clear preference by President Trump to ensure Taiwan does not become an obstacle to his ambitions as it relates to China,” he said.

Still, Taiwan’s security relationship with the United States remains robust. Officials and experts say working ties between government departments have remained steady, even deepened.

During Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang military exercises last month, American advisers were more visible than in past years. At a recent briefing with reporters, Taiwan’s defense minister, Wellington Koo, spoke coyly of growing numbers of “American English teachers,” a euphemism for the U.S. military advisers whose presence rankles Beijing.

“Our friends in the U.S. government understand how important continued arms sales are for Taiwan’s defense,” Chen Ming-chi, a deputy minister in Taiwan’s foreign ministry who handles relations with the United States, said in an interview.

Taiwan’s importance as an American trading partner has also grown sharply; this year it surpassed China as the third biggest source of U.S. imports, behind Mexico and Canada, according to U.S. figures. The bulk of those imports are semiconductors and other high-tech equipment sustaining the artificial intelligence boom in the United States. Taiwanese officials hope this growth will ultimately help entrench American support.

“We are probably the most cooperative partner in the whole world when it comes to tariffs and investment in the United States,” Mr. Chen said.

Mr. Trump often complains about Taiwan’s dominance in making advanced semiconductors, raising his long-held, and widely debunked, accusation that the island pilfered chip-making know-how from the United States. “They got stolen from us and they were brought to Taiwan,” Mr. Trump said last month in a radio interview.

But displacing Taiwan as a chief source of advanced chips is unlikely, even as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, the main global chip maker, expands production in the United States, experts say. TSMC has said it will spend $265 billion on its plants in Arizona. But Taiwan’s dense networks of suppliers and engineering talent remains difficult to replicate.

“Building structural interdependence with our most critical ally provides the ultimate assurance for our national security,” said Jeremy Chih-Cheng Chang, the director of economic security studies at the Research Institute for Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology in Taipei, which receives funding from the Taiwanese government.

“Presidents come and go," said Mr. Chang, “but Silicon Valley and Wall Street remain constant.”

item.title: At 92, the Bard of Bollywood Is Still Writing About Love
item.description:
In one of the most beloved songs written by the Indian poet known as Gulzar, two lovers conspire to capture time, to steal it away for themselves.

The voices that render his words in the Bollywood musical inspired by Shakespeare’s Othello are melancholic, playful. But the song, “O Saathi Re,” has an urgency: The lovers’ plan involves entrapping the tired sun on a day’s end before it slips down into a river.

You hold it there, I will throw in the net

You carry it on your back, I will lend a hand.

Over his six decades in Mumbai, the seaside metropolis where he found shelter as a teenage refugee, Gulzar has had an outsize hand in shaping the idea of tender romance in India.

He has put his imagination to children’s books, short stories, and volumes of poetry that have only grown in ambition. Through it all, he has maintained a wonder at the beauty in the mundane.

In late June, I went to see him at his home. As I waited in his driveway to be let in, the steady thumping of the monsoon showers was the only thing that disturbed the quiet in his sloped lane.

“The whole city is wet, isn’t that a very interesting feeling?” he asked me, with a joyful grin. “I think it’s very interesting — something falling from above your head in the clouds. They’re playing with you.”

Gulzar’s poetic outlook made his mark on India’s popular film industry. And Bollywood gave him a livelihood, and the visual and musical wings to travel across the divides of a region of nearly two billion people.

In addition to directing over a dozen films of his own and writing the screenplays for many others, he has provided lyrics to more than 150 Bollywood musicals. You could be singing any evergreen song of the past few decades in India and chances are strong that the words carrying you away are Gulzar’s.

At 92 now, he is still up with the sun and at his desk every morning, tucked away on the ground floor of his two-story home.

“The sky opens up, like a roll of fabric,” he said. “Nothing like seeing a sunrise.”

He maintains the kind of discipline that has allowed him to produce a body of work — and the major awards that followed — too enormous to tally.

For one of his recent projects, he collected contemporary poetry from nearly 300 poets writing in three dozen languages from across India — making it all accessible to a wider audience through renditions in Hindi and English. “A Poem a Day,” as the tome published by HarperCollins is titled, took a decade of meticulous work. It was his promise to a group of students who had complained to him that poetry, relegated to textbooks, was no longer relevant to their daily lives.

We spoke during our visit about his latest book, which is an ode to Mumbai, about his childhood, and about the changing nature of storytelling in Indian cinema in the age of reel-attention-spans. His eyes lit up when he talked about tennis, which he played nearly every morning until two years ago, when he was about to turn 90.

“You know, Federer’s backhand,” he said, “that swing of his backhand, single-handed, was fascinating. Nobody has reached that.”

In my six years reporting in India, two themes have consumed me greatly. In meeting the increasingly few remaining survivors of the bloody 1947 partition that birthed this modern state, I have been moved by their quiet endurance in the face of deep trauma. I have equally been fascinated by the country’s arts and cinema, in how they conjure the idea of nationhood and shared culture across a vastly diverse nation.

Gulzar’s life and Gulzar’s art brought the two together. As my time in India was concluding, I wanted to hear his reflections on both.

A survivor of that gruesome period of bloodletting at the partition of India that created Pakistan, he has drawn on influences and languages from across India, refining and reinventing his art decade after decade to build a body of work known for its tenderness.

All along he has maintained a certain childlike joy in the world around him, his crisp wit a central part of his art.

Rakhshanda Jalil, who translated several of Gulzar’s books into English, was on a flight to Canada with the poet around 2019. Dr. Jalil was busy working on her laptop next to Gulzar, who was in the window seat.

“The sheep, the sheep,” Gulzar repeated to himself, loud enough that she could hear. “They are fighting among each other.”

Dr. Jalil said she looked up confused.

“Don’t these clouds look like sheep that are getting entangled among themselves?”

That same simple wonder at the everyday characterizes his poetry and the iconic lyrics he has added to Indian music decade after decade.

There is the hit breakup song “Mera Kuchh Samaan,” hauntingly simple, about a lover asking for the return of her few remaining items. Song after song that you find on Indian dance floors — from the rhythmic, train-top “Chaiyya Chaiyya” that has become a timeless anthem of sorts, to the upbeat “Jai Ho” that has many, arms spread, roaring to the skies. And, of course, the cheeky “Dil To Bachcha Hai Ji,” about an aging lover who insists that he is afraid to sleep alone because his “heart is still a child.”

He was born Sampooran Singh Kalra, to a Sikh family in the village of Dina, in what lies in Pakistan today. There is confusion about his exact year of birth, but he thinks it was 1934. His mother died when he was months old and he grew up in a household of seven half-siblings.

His father ran a fabric shop in the village and had opened another in Delhi, about 400 miles away. While the rest of the family stayed in the village, he took the child with him to Delhi in the 1940s, where he attended school and helped in the shop.

In the evenings, the boy retreated to the shop’s storeroom, where he would sleep, but only after devouring Urdu detective novels by the lantern light. The stall across the street that he would rent the books from became his earliest literary influence, introducing him to writings from across India and around the world translated into Urdu.

His life changed when the owner one day recommended an Urdu translation of “The Gardener,” a collection of poems by Rabindranath Tagore, India’s first Nobel laureate. He read and reread the book, renting it repeatedly until it became the first book he ever stole.

But poetry was also something that was slowly drilled into him at the Delhi school he attended, the United Christian School. His literature teacher, a Muslim cleric, encouraged students to memorize couplets. Gulzar described the process as akin to imbibing religious texts.

“The couplets that you memorize,” he said, “when its meaning starts getting into you, that is how the learning comes into you, that is how education comes in.”

As one of his methods, his teacher would split the class in half for a Bait-Baazi, a competition of couplets. A member of each team had to think of a couplet starting with the letter that the previous team had ended theirs with.

“Sometimes, we used to cheat in some places,” he said with a smile. “Twisting the ends, changing the order of a word.”

He would also be ready with his own poems, signed using the pen-name Gulzar.

The partition of India in 1947 changed everything, with hundreds of thousands of people killed and millions forced to leave their homes in a population swap across a new border.

Punjab saw the worst of the violence. Gulzar’s siblings in the village in Dina had to pack up and come to Delhi. But the violence did not spare Delhi, with the teenager haunted by bodies strewed across streets. For nearly two decades after, he would wake up with nightmares. The trauma, the anguish of his early days would forever remain an emotional backdrop to his art.

“The writing becomes your shelter — to express yourself and relieve yourself, to purge it out,” he told me.

Gulzar was sent to Mumbai as a teenager by his father, who felt the Delhi house had grown too crowded. The family had taken in many other relatives who had arrived at Delhi’s refugee camps.

In Mumbai, as he pursued his studies, he worked many years at a car garage, where he put his mind to mixing paint for the exact shade needed to touch up vehicles damaged in accidents. He dropped his traditional turban and cut his hair — infringements on Sikh tradition that his father was not happy about.

Books continued to remain his refuge. He found company in leftist circles of theater artists and writers who were active in the city in the 1950s.

It was a friend from those circles that facilitated his opening into Indian cinema. The legendary director, Bimal Roy, needed someone to write a song. Young Gulzar was brought to him in what would become the beginning of an illustrious career.

His first song, for a black and white film, was about capturing the inner thoughts of a woman madly in love. “I have lost something in me after finding you,” she sings.

In the decades that followed, Gulzar expanded from writing lyrics to directing over a dozen of his own films.

The film industry also gave him a family. He married the acclaimed actress Rakhee. While the couple separated soon after marriage — “the longest short story of my life,” as Gulzar has described the marriage — they raised a daughter, Meghna, who is also an accomplished filmmaker. For each of Meghna’s first 13 birthdays, Gulzar presented her with a new book of children’s stories that he had written.

No matter his success in filmmaking and song writing, he never stopped turning out books of poetry that he felt could more fully express his creativity.

“A poem is your own commitment, your own thought, and it germinates within you”

He stopped directing after his last film in 1999 and has since been entirely dedicated to writing, and largely poetry. He is increasingly selective about writing lyrics for films, only entertaining requests from a couple of directors who understand poetry and allow him the freedom to write the way he wants, he said.

His daily routine, simple and spare, is built around his writing.

He wakes up at dawn and is lights out around 10 p.m. While advancing age has deprived him of activities like tennis (he still watches every major match on television), he builds each day around reading, writing and solitude. He often fondly repeats a line from his wife, Rakhee: “If you weren’t a poet, you would be quite an ordinary man.”

In 2013, during a rare period of calm between the fractious nations of India and Pakistan, he went to Pakistan and made a brief visit to Dina — more than 70 years after he had left the village. In a note to Dina’s residents, he wrote about how overwhelmed he was by the flood of memories.

“All I wanted was a moment of solitude,” he said in the note, “so I could sit and weep.”

When I asked him if he still thinks of his home village, he turned the question into a meditation about how the experiences of life shape us — about beginnings and roots that may no longer be visible but still ground us.

“Life brushes you every moment when you are living. It’s up to you if your antennae are open — what affects you,” he said.

His eyes gleamed; an image had come to him. He leaned forward on his desk.

“Oh my god, look at that leaf flying, coming, coming, down, down, and falls down from the tree.”

He asked me to think of the image — “this leaf, this fresh leaf, why it left its branch” — at the precise moment mid-fall. And he wondered about the cycle before and after the fall, about personifying the journey. What was this longing to join others in touching “mother earth,” where its roots are?

“I find a poem in it, in that leaf falling down. You may not,” he said. “But I can make you aware. And next time, when you see the leaf, if you remember — ‘My god, see, look, it’s floating, it’s coming down’ — you will react to it.”

The more I read about India, the more amazing it is with all the myriad and wonderful peoples, ideas and cultures.

I was blown away that he spent a whole decade collecting poetry from across this vast country written in dozens of languages, and translated that poetry into one book so it reaches a wider audience. Even more special was how much he emphasized to me his own learning doing the project — that he walked away with so much more than the project gives the reader, he said. That all his life, he has been open to absorbing from so many languages and literary traditions in india

item.title: The Fuel That Feeds Europe’s Far Right: Nostalgia and Lost Pride
item.description:
The rise of a far-right party in Germany, the Alternative for Germany, represents a skewing of history, fueled by its own, sometimes imaginary vision of the past. It feeds, analysts say, on widespread alienation from a liberal, multicultural, united Germany committed to the memory of the Holocaust and Nazi crimes.

The AfD is now the most popular party nationwide, polls say, close to governing a German state for the first time, and did well again in two more state elections on Sunday. It has benefited from economic and industrial decline and a sense of insecurity, which the party blames on the extensive migration of young Muslims in the last decade.

The party came first in the small eastern German state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania and a good third in Berlin, while the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz did poorly, in what he himself called “a disaster.” The results will heighten talk of the party’s replacing the unpopular chancellor before the end of his term.

The AfD has thrived on a key element that ties most populist parties together, especially those of the far right: nostalgia for a society and nation lost to time, even if they exist only in gilded memory or fantasy.

“We live in a world today of fragmentation and growing inequality, no longer with unifying themes or a unifying narrative,” said Mohamed A. El-Erian, an economist at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania.

That sense of insecurity, analysts say, is driving many people to yearn for the narratives they do know, especially in the past, when life is remembered as simpler, family structures seemed more defined, and Western nations were largely Christian and less diverse.

Across Europe, far-right leaders have painted that idea of the past as preferable to the present, downplaying or dismissing inconvenient facts, such as Mussolini in Italy, collaboration with the Nazis, Soviet occupation or the inequalities of Margaret Thatcher’s Britain.

France’s far-right party, the National Rally, ahead in the polls for next year’s crucial presidential election, has made French identity central to its ideology, which includes praising heroes like Jeanne d’Arc and downplaying the Vichy regime.

Its emphasis on national values, assimilation and state preferences for citizens is largely shared by other far-right parties, including the Party of Freedom of Geert Wilders in the Netherlands, the Sweden Democrats and the Reform U.K. party of Nigel Farage.

Behind tough positions on restricting immigration — and the deportation, or “remigration,” of illegal immigrants and criminals — these parties envision a threat to their culture and identity. They see national or even European culture as largely white and Christian, threatened by globalization, Islam and the dilution of nationalism in institutions like the European Union.

Leaders of the American MAGA movement have expressed similar fears, with Vice President JD Vance worrying about “civilizational death,” both in Europe and the United States, and arguing that ancestry means more than adherence to a national creed.

“I think the people whose ancestors fought in the Civil War have a hell of a lot more claim over America than the people who say” anyone who does not agree with “progressive liberalism” does not belong in the country, he said last year.

In his recent book, “Communion,” Mr. Vance asserts that the shift from “Western Christian civilization” to “secular global liberalism” is to blame for rising racial strife, the erosion of traditional marriage and a decline in population growth.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, too, has emphasized Christianity as a “sacred inheritance, an unbreakable link between the Old World and the New.”

The yearning for a proud identity is particularly strong in the former East Germany, which was essentially annexed in a peaceful takeover in 1989. As the country unified, West Germans arrived as a new elite to run businesses, or shut them down, and as much as a quarter of the population moved west, including many young women.

In a conversation in Weimar, in Thuringia, and where German democracy collapsed before the Nazis, Anna Wenske, 69, spoke of the East German identity as something lost.

“It was more German,” she said. “Not little America, like the West.”

Key AfD figures like Björn Höcke have played into that persistent division, suggesting that West Germans are not even German anymore, just colonized Americans, said Steffen Mau, a sociologist who was born in East Germany.

“They give people with an inferiority complex the feeling that they were better Germans, and that they are authentic, they are the future,” he said.

Many East Germans felt that they resisted their Soviet occupiers more than West Germans resisted the culture of their occupiers, especially the Americans. Communist East Germany cast itself as the inheritor of the resistance to Hitler, historians have said, and hence did not embrace the culture of guilt that dominated the West after the war.

For many young people in Germany, who are voting in large numbers for the far left or the far right, the war was not their responsibility, and the AfD’s appeal to highlight national accomplishment, not collective crime, is attractive.

Much as President Trump has pushed U.S. institutions to downplay slavery and highlight heroes like George Washington, the AfD wants to remake education, museums and public media to downplay German guilt and emphasize German pride and greatness.

“More Bismarck, less Hitler,” Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the AfD’s deputy state chairman and education spokesman in Saxony-Anhalt, has said.

Germany is having “a psychodrama over its own history,” said Yascha Mounk, a German-American political scientist. “The debate over right-wing populism is in part what to make of German history,” he said.

The AfD, he said, wants to abandon the dominant “Erinnerungskultur,” or Culture of Remembrance, about the crimes of the Nazis, for a different, prouder future.

What the shift from memory culture really represents, said Ivan Krastev, a political scientist and analyst, “is the end of the long political 20th century.” Responsibility for the Nazis, he said, “cannot be used to stabilize Germany’s political system any longer.”

In Eastern Germany especially, he said, the nostalgia is not for Communism or the Nazi regime. Instead, the yearning is for the huge numbers of people who left the East, and the quiet life remembered by those who stayed.

“They are nostalgic for the world that they believe they understood, and now they’re living in a world that they do not understand,” Mr. Krastev said. “The pride people felt in their own lives was not honored, and people deprived of their pride are very easily tempted by political parties that start to talk about pride, grandeur and greatness.”

Echoes of the same arguments were clear in talks given at the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy by Jordan Bardella, the deputy to France’s National Rally, and by Roberto Vannacci, a former general who has started an Italian political party, National Future, which is further to the right than that of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

The far-right speakers were far from unopposed: Centrists at the annual economic forum attacked them, accusing them of tilting toward fascism, and cited François Mitterrand’s last speech as French president, when he said that in Europe, “nationalism is war.”

Where voters stand between these competing forces will be put to the test with key elections next year in France, Italy, Poland and Spain, all of which have strong far-right parties trying to push politics in their direction.

The West has grown complacent about democracy and “started taking it for granted,” said Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel laureate in economics and the author of “What Happened to Liberal Democracy?”

Democratic backsliding and the rise of populist politics are “very much driven by the failures of liberal democracy,” he said.

The two broad lines of that failure, he said, are economic — with rising inequality and the neglect of efforts to spread wealth — and the rise of what he said were “top-down cultural politics,” which has treated less-educated and less-advantaged voters and their concerns with contempt, opening a void for far-right parties to fill.

To a large extent, what is happening in Germany is an international phenomenon, noted John Kampfner, a British analyst of Germany, where he is also a citizen. “Each of these populist movements have their specificities but follow similar tramlines,” he said.

“A population that feels insecure,” he said, “that equates globalization and transnational identity with insecurity, is very open to this kind of identitarian politics from the nationalist conservative point of view.”

I have been fascinated by the modern version of the far right and MAGA, too, harkening to a gilded, sometimes fantastical past shorn of national mistakes, tragedies and crimes, when life apparently to them seemed simpler, clearer and certainly less confusing and diverse. In Eastern Germany especially, the past is another country, peacefully taken over, which is patronized by the westerners. History... rhymes.

A year ago, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, the country’s de facto ruler, and President Trump signed a strategic defense agreement. The Saudi leader has repeatedly asked Mr. Trump to intervene militarily against the Houthis, part of the so-called axis of resistance led by Iran, along with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza.

But Mr. Trump has wavered. He initially rebuffed the Saudi requests, then, over the weekend, told the Pentagon to prepare airstrikes, only to reverse course and decide to hold off, according to Trump administration officials.

Here is how the war restarted, why the Houthis were able to gain ground so quickly, and what the renewed fighting means for anyone with a stake in the conflict.

Yemen was plunged into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis, Shiite Muslims who describe themselves as an anti-imperialist force battling foreign influence, swept into the capital, Sanaa, and pushed out the internationally recognized government. Soon after, a Saudi-led military coalition, backing the government, began a bombing campaign, plunging the impoverished nation into a devastating conflict.

The two sides agreed to a fragile truce in 2022, but that has unraveled in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

In July, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian plane from landing. The group also balked at longstanding restrictions imposed on Yemeni airspace and declared a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, obstructing a route that the Saudi government relied on to export oil after Iran stymied shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

A major turning point in the Houthi advance occurred this month, when Houthi forces captured Mokha, a strategic Red Sea port, and Perim Island, located in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a narrow waterway that is a crucial route for global trade. Control of the territories put the group in a stronger position to attack passing ships.

Last week, the group sharply escalated its attacks on Saudi Arabia, launching missiles and drones at the capital, Riyadh. The Houthis described the attacks as retaliation against hundreds of Saudi airstrikes and other attacks in Yemen over recent weeks. Saudi officials have neither addressed those allegations, nor acknowledged a Houthi claim to have shot down a Saudi fighter jet.

When the truce was reached four years ago, the Houthis said they had won the war and entrenched their rule over northern Yemen. But since then, the economic situation in areas under their control has worsened, spurring civilian resentment and putting political pressure on the group.

The Houthis blame Saudi Arabia’s interventions for the suffering in their territory, analysts say. In recent months, the group has demanded that restrictions on planes and ships entering Houthi territory be lifted, including U.N. inspections. The militia has also insisted that Saudi Arabia pay war reparations and fully withdraw from Yemen — meaning the end of Saudi support for the internationally recognized government.

“The Houthis have no incentive to de-escalate,” said Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni researcher and policy adviser. He added that Houthi leaders hope that maintaining pressure on Saudi Arabia will lead to more political concessions and add to their authority.

Iran has also played a key role in the militia’s push, according to Baraa Shiban, a researcher on Yemen and the Gulf at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based research organization.

The Houthis are an Iranian ally, rather than a complete proxy. The group balances its relations with Iran alongside its own calculations.

But if the Houthis are able to further disrupt the global economy and increase pressure on U.S. gas prices, that would give Iran more leverage over Mr. Trump, Mr. Shiban added. Iran is counting on escalation in Yemen to drag the United States deeper into the regional war and “put more pressure on the Trump administration,” he said.

The Saudi-backed government of Yemen is the main bulwark against the Houthis, and nominally controls a swath of southern and eastern Yemen.

But throughout the civil war, the government has become weaker and more fragmented. Today, it is effectively a motley coalition of armed groups, overseen by a “Presidential Leadership Council” of eight men. Many of them distrust one another and have competing political goals, although they share a desire to defeat the Houthis.

They are also beholden to Saudi Arabia, which supports the government financially and militarily, and the kingdom leaves little space for its Yemeni allies to make their own decisions.

By contrast, the Houthis have more authority to act independently of Iran. They still rely on Iran for the most sophisticated drones and ballistic missiles, but they have been able to use artificial intelligence and other tools to make advanced weaponry themselves and developed their own supply chains to do so, analysts say.

“The Saudis are used to treating their Yemeni partners as clients, like hired help. They pay them, but they give them no agency,” said Abdulghani al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, a research group.

During the past few months, as the Houthis stepped up attacks against Saudi interests, some Yemeni government officials have described an opportunity opening up for a counteroffensive against the militia. The Saudi government tried to unite the factions in Yemen and stepped up military support.

But the first test of those efforts — the battle for Mokha and the Bab al-Mandab Strait — was an abject failure, analysts say. The different forces on the government side struggled to effectively coordinate with one another while the Houthis were unified under a highly centralized leadership.

Saudi officials have revealed little about their plans, even as they have repeatedly sought more military support from the United States. While the Trump administration has so far withheld this backing, Andy Burnham, the prime minister of Britain, said on Monday that the Royal Air Force would provide air-to-air refueling support for Saudi aircraft for a limited number of weeks, The Associated Press and BBC reported.

The kingdom has many reasons to be reluctant to return to war. Its previous bombing campaign in Yemen turned into a costly quagmire that contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Yemenis from violence, hunger and disease. Diplomacy has also failed to definitively end the conflict.

But increasingly, some Saudi officials believe that they have no choice but to confront the militia, analysts say.

“The Saudis have a growing kind of belief that peace with the Houthis is impossible,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research group. “They try to buy them, they try to bomb them, they try to fight them, they try to visit them, they try to invite them. None of this has worked.”

Even as some observers hope that the conflict can be resolved quickly, Mr. Al-Muslimi fears the worst.

“There’s a lot of people who are excited for it or think that this will be a quick and fast war, but I have heard that line about almost every war in Yemen,” he said. “This is going to be a bloody, horrible war.”
