item.title: U.N. General Assembly to Confront Familiar Crises, New Conflicts and A.I.
item.description:
World leaders will converge in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly with the Middle East in turmoil, war raging between Russia and Ukraine, old alliances in peril, energy prices rising and scientists warning that artificial intelligence could imperil humanity.

“It would be hard to imagine a scenario as threatening as the one we’re facing right now,” acknowledged António Guterres, who has served two terms as the U.N. secretary general since 2017 and will step down at the end of December.

The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and its reverberations on the world economy and oil supplies will be a major topic. And Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, is expected to implore world leaders not to forget his country.

But for the first time at the world body, the threat posed by artificial intelligence has jumped to the top of the agenda. U.N. leaders plan to seek global cooperation for guardrails around the rapidly advancing technology.

Against the backdrop of these challenges, the U.N. is searching for its next leader, who will take the helm in January. Seven candidates are in the running after Michelle Bachelet, former Chilean president and ex-high commissioner of the U.N.’s Human Rights Council, dropped out. But so far no clear front-runner has emerged, diplomats said, because the United Nations Security Council, the body responsible for selecting the secretary general, has not reached a consensus.

Mr. Guterres will deliver his final address to the General Assembly on Tuesday, and he is expected to close his tenure by urging world leaders to defend international law, protect human rights, invest in sustainable development and push for peace.

“At a time when the world faces three existential threats — runaway artificial intelligence, the climate crisis and the intolerable deepening of inequalities — international cooperation is more necessary than ever,” Mr. Guterres said at a recent news conference.

He said that when he took charge of the institution years ago no one could have predicted where the world would be as it is today, roiled by conflicts and facing a multitude of crises like climate change and the seemingly unrestrained growth of artificial intelligence.

The U.N. has defined the theme of this year’s gathering as “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformations: A United Nations That Delivers for All.” Trust and transformation have been among the biggest challenges for the U.N. as it has faced questions of relevance from donors and the public, experienced severe funding cutbacks from the Trump administration and made efforts to streamline its operations. At the same time, its 15-member Security Council stands paralyzed by divisions among its five permanent members with veto-holding powers.

Still, while the organization said in January that it was facing imminent financial collapse and would run out of money by the summer if member states — namely the United States, its top donor — didn’t pay their annual dues, it has survived.

Last week, the United States paid $725 million to the U.N. as part of its dues for the regular budget and $102 million for peacekeeping, but it still owes $1.3 billion in annual dues, said Farhan Haq, a U.N. spokesman.

Many U.N. staff members and diplomats had expressed anxiety that President Trump could withdraw from the organization altogether, given his exit from U.N. agencies like the World Health Organization and defunding of some programs as part of a policy to cut foreign aid significantly. Analysts said last year that the U.N. was in a “free fall,” as it observed its 80th anniversary.

But those fears have not materialized. Analysts said that while the U.N. was still facing a crisis, the United States had remained engaged, albeit seeking to change and bend the institution to the administration’s vision.

Richard Gowan, a U.N. expert at the International Crisis Group., said of the United Nations, “It is still standing, and if you compare the U.N. to some of the really bad periods during the Cold War, it’s still actually far more active than it was in its darkest hours.”

He added, “But every single year it’s a little bit less relevant; it’s a little bit more under restraint.”

Mr. Trump is set to speak to the General Assembly on Tuesday morning, the first day of the gathering. Last year, he lectured the United Nations and other countries about how they were failing and aired a list of grievances.

“Your countries are going to hell,” he said.

This year, he will be facing a world rattled by his imposition of tariffs, his open disdain for allies and the instability resulting from his war against Iran.

The biggest hurdle for the U.N. in resolving conflicts in the past few years has been the geopolitical divisions among the five permanent powers of the Security Council: the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain. The Council, which is in charge of preventing global conflict and safeguarding stability, has been frozen over the wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran because action has been blocked by permanent members with stakes in the fighting.

The Ukraine war is more than four years old, the conflicts in Sudan over three years old, the one in Gaza closing in on three years and the United States’ war with Iran nearing its seventh month. The conflict in Iran has sent energy and oil prices soaring and has upended supply chains that rely on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia have intensified fighting in the past few weeks with another critical waterway, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, in the Indian Ocean, under threat.

“There is clearly a vacuum here in terms of dealing with these growing number of wars we have and other crises,” said Robert A. Wood, a U.S. ambassador to the U.N. during the Biden administration. “It is critical that we get a next secretary general who has experience, and Rolodex, and kind of energy and background in managing, not only dealing with great powers, but in dealing with major international crises.”

Among the speeches by leaders that will be watched closely will be the ones by President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran; Mr. Zelensky; and Venezuela’s leader, Delcy Rodríguez, who will be making her debut on the world stage after the United States captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro. Others of note will be by leaders of the Arab countries in the Persian Gulf; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel; and the Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas, who will address the Assembly virtually for a second year because the United States denied the Palestinian delegation visas.

This year, discussion of a possible two-state solution for Israel and Palestinians is expected to be more low-key than in the past, with France, Britain, Canada and Saudi Arabia hosting a session on Thursday on the sidelines of the General Assembly meeting.

A notable number of world leaders will be absent from the General Assembly. Xi Jinping of China is traveling to Washington to see Mr. Trump on Thursday, and the meeting is expected to overshadow the speeches at the Assembly in New York.

The leaders of two nations from the so-called global south — India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, and South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa — will also not attend.

The Security Council will hold a session on Ukraine, as it has done for the past four years during the General Assembly meeting, and this year it has drawn new criticism that European members of the Council have ignored other pressing conflicts every year to keep the spotlight on Ukraine during the high-level week.

Despite their global repercussions, Iran and the conflict in the Persian Gulf are not on the Council’s public agenda this week. Arab countries in the Gulf are expected to hold a closed-door meeting with Council members and Mr. Trump on the sidelines, diplomats said.

The Council will discuss A.I. and the threats it poses to global security and stability. Mr. Guterres will also host a side event on Monday to urge countries to create global regulations for the technology, and a private, invitation-only event at the U.N. that brings together heads of states and leaders of A.I. to debate how to govern the field.

But a clash of opinions and visions is expected.

The United States, China and Russia have indicated that they oppose external rules on their own development of A.I. technology, and Mr. Trump recently denounced such efforts as a “sick conspiracy.”

Mr. Guterres said the world cannot “afford a race to the bottom on A.I. safety.” He added, “We need guardrails to build trust, and that make A.I. safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the center.”

item.title: An Election Engineered to Send a Message That Putin’s Grip Remains Firm
item.description:
As near-final results came in on Monday for Russia’s first parliamentary elections since President Vladimir V. Putin invaded Ukraine, the Kremlin largely let the numbers do the talking. United Russia, the ruling party, was on track to win more seats than ever. Turnout, according to preliminary statistics, was the highest for a parliamentary vote in 15 years.

The elections were engineered in various ways to achieve the desired results, according to analysts, who cautioned that the numbers shouldn’t be read as an expression of how the Russian public feels. But they can be viewed for the message that the Kremlin was trying to send: Russia is rallying around Mr. Putin, who remains firmly in control despite the war’s challenges.

“The turnout categorically shows that the country supports the commander in chief, the country supports its army at war, and the country believes that we are acting justly, and that right is on our side,” Yevgeny Poddubny, a war correspondent for state television who ran as a United Russia candidate, said during a talk show on Sunday after voting had concluded.

It was a message designed for both domestic and international consumption, as the election authorities said United Russia had won as many as 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma and claimed about 58 percent of the vote. That was higher than even state-run pollsters had projected.

Dmitri Kulikov, a pro-Kremlin commentator on state television, cheered the election result as a contribution to coming victory in the war. He called it a message to Western countries that he said were trying to destroy Russia by arming Ukraine.

“You know how they love to ‘send a message,’ right?” he said. “Well, we are sending them a very clear message: Don’t hold your breath. Better back off.”

While United Russia is a primary instrument of Mr. Putin’s power, he usually keeps a distance from the party, casting himself as an independent arbiter above politics. But this year, the party leaned in to its connection to Mr. Putin, who gave a clear endorsement at the party congress and was shown on camera with the party’s top candidates. In their ads, the candidates also leaned into the association with the president.

Mr. Putin, however, was publicly silent on Monday about the election results. The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said only that Mr. Putin would meet soon with the head of Russia’s election commission and the leaders of the parties that will enter the Duma, as the lower house of Parliament is known.

The election came just as Mr. Putin’s fortunes have begun to turn in the war, with Ukraine running short of air defenses and Russia employing new jet-powered drones. The U.S.-Israeli war in Iran has helped drive up the price of oil, one of Russia’s biggest exports, alleviating the challenge to Moscow’s finances posed by runaway war spending.

Still, Mr. Putin has struggled in recent months with rising discontent over declining economic prospects, widening internet restrictions and increasing Ukrainian drone and missile strikes. That prompted questions about whether those feelings would somehow show up in the election results.

But the vote, as expected, was a highly stage-managed affair, limited to approved parties, with some people forced to cast ballots. Russia also has strict laws on demonstrating against or criticizing the war, and it has ensured that antiwar figures remaining in the country continue to face pressure from the authorities.

In August, Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko, the only party running on an antiwar platform, from appearing on the ballot, as polls showed the party gaining in popularity and possibly poised to win enough votes to enter Parliament.

Some of the party’s candidates were able to stay on the ballot in their individual districts, but none won. The party did meet the threshold to get into the regional legislature in Novgorod, near St. Petersburg. That region was the only one that allowed the party on the ballot in a regional election.

The party’s chairman, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrated his contempt for what he described as an unfair election by depositing a ballot at his polling station with the words “For freedom yes Yabloko” written across the text in green marker. Eight Yabloko members are in prison for expressing antiwar views, including Lev Shlosberg, who was sentenced to 11 years for “discrediting the Russian military.”

To a large degree, the election demonstrated that Mr. Putin’s autocratic system was still functioning and able to deliver the result he sought, despite a small element of unpredictability from the rising discontent, said Tatiana Stanovaya, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

“There was a certain margin — not a very large one — that created a risk of things potentially going wrong,” Ms. Stanovaya said. “The question was whether the system and the regime were strong and stable enough to deliver the results Putin wanted to see, despite these new risks.”

She said the system had proved its ability “to control the situation without any surprises, despite the rising antiwar sentiment, despite anxiety and the decline in the approval ratings of the authorities.”

Mr. Putin’s government repeatedly emphasized that Russia was carrying out the election despite difficult circumstances, an implicit criticism of Ukraine, which by law cannot hold elections under martial law.

Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said on Sunday that Ukraine had carried out the biggest attack of the war on the Russian capital on the last of three days of voting. The city’s largest oil refinery, which Ukraine hit earlier in the year, was struck again. The Russian authorities also asserted that the election had withstood cyberattacks from several countries, including Ukraine.

Ms. Stanovaya said that while the election results had not been an accurate reflection of Russian popular opinion, the voting did confirm that Mr. Putin continued to have a base of support, albeit not as big as the authorities claimed.

“Of course, United Russia doesn’t have 57 percent, but it doesn’t have 10 percent, either,” Ms. Stanovaya said. “A significant portion of the population did, after all, vote for the ruling party.”

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Strikes on Alleged Drug Boats Could Be Criminal, U.N. Expert Says
item.description:
Airstrikes by the United States on alleged drug-smuggling boats, which have killed more than 220 people, violate international law and plausibly constitute crimes against humanity, a United Nations legal expert said in a paper published on Monday.

Ben Saul, the U.N. special rapporteur monitoring human rights in the context of counterterrorism, also challenged the legality of the U.S. seizure of Nicolás Maduro, then the president of Venezuela, and aspects of U.S. collaboration with Latin American states under the Trump administration’s “Shield of the Americas” initiative.

Mr. Saul focused particularly on 68 military strikes carried out by the U.S. military on what it said were drug-carrying vessels in the Caribbean and Pacific between September 2025 and August 2026, killing at least 223 people.

The attacks have been part of a military offensive designated “Southern Spear” launched in September 2025 with the stated aim of interdicting drug smuggling by organizations linked to drug cartels. The United States has not offered evidence that the boats carried drugs, but even if they were, experts have questioned the legality of the attacks.

“There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law,” Mr. Saul, a professor of international law at Australia’s University of Sydney, concluded.

The Pentagon had no immediate response to Mr. Saul’s report.

This month, which was not covered by his report, the Pentagon has announced two more strikes, including one on Saturday, raising the total to 70 vessels and 234 people killed.

Even if the crews of the boats were members of criminal groups that the Trump administration has designated as terrorist organizations, they had not mounted any armed attack on the United States that would give it the right of self-defense, Mr. Saul wrote. “Drug trafficking is not equivalent to a military attack,” he wrote.

Moreover, the airstrikes on these vessels could not be considered as a necessary or proportionate response given the availability of other means to intercept them, he added.

Mr. Saul’s paper adds to the growing critiques from lawyers and human rights experts of the Trump administration, which withdrew the United States from the U.N. Human Rights Council and says it gives no weight to the council’s statements. A U.N. fact-finding mission that last week found U.S. airstrikes on Iran may have amounted to war crimes took note of public statements by American officials, including Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, that it said were dismissive of U.S. obligations under international law.

U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk last year condemned the attacks on alleged drug trafficking vessels as a violation of international law, and called for investigation and, possibly, prosecution of those responsible. Mr. Saul also raised the question of possible criminal liability for those responsible for issuing or carrying out illegal orders.

But Mr. Saul’s paper went farther in challenging the legal basis for much of the wider U.S. strategy pursued by the Trump administration to combat narco-terrorism in the region, including the U.S. military’s seizure of Mr. Maduro in January. He was charged with involvement in large-scale drug trafficking.

The seizure of Mr. Maduro, in which at least 75 people were killed, constituted a prohibited use of force, Mr. Saul wrote.

U.S. efforts to expand multilateral and bilateral cooperation in the fight against narcotics trafficking, under the Shield of the Americas initiative promoted “a highly securitized response without explicit commitments to human rights and international law, or to addressing root causes of organized crime such as poverty, corruption and State weakness,” he wrote.

Mr. Saul concluded his paper with a stinging critique of the ineffectiveness of the U.S. strategy. The Drug Enforcement Administration had concluded that the military action had not reduced the supply, price or purity of cocaine in the United States, he noted. Much of the cocaine arrives in container ships that are not routinely inspected, not the small boats targeted in airstrikes.

Military attacks have focused on cocaine smuggling and not on the fentanyl and opioids responsible for most U.S. drug-overdose deaths and not for the most part transported by sea from Venezuela, he added.

item.title: Spectre of Rogue A.I. Looms Over U.N. Talks on Digital Cooperation
item.description:
Hundreds of diplomats, business executives, tech experts and academics gathered Monday to wrestle with questions about how to ensure humanity is not someday destroyed by rogue machines.

The talks took place as the U.N. opened the 81st session of its General Assembly, at a conference about global cooperation on artificial intelligence. And while it is only the second time diplomats and dignitaries have met for the event, called Digital Cooperation Day, the stakes are already much higher than they were when they gathered a year ago.

With fears of unchecked technology at a fever pitch, some took the opportunity to warn against passivity.

“We talk about A.I. as though it were a weather event, a storm,” said Amandeep Singh Gill, the U.N.’s under secretary general and special envoy for emerging technologies. But, he said, “A.I. is not an uncontrollable force of nature — it is built by humans and it can be controlled by humans.”

The actor and director Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who is serving as the U.N.’s first global advocate for “human-centric digital governance,” pushed back against what he said were narratives and vocabulary about A.I. that gave the false impression that humanity was helpless in the face of a “new technological revolution.”

Some tech companies, he said, have appeared to be distancing themselves from the very tools they built. When they have disclosed disconcerting incidents, such as recent hacks into other businesses, they have characterized them as executed by “a rogue swarm of A.I. agents,” Mr. Gordon-Levitt said.

He said he believed in the power of A.I. to improve lives around the world, but he warned, “We need to remember who is at the center of that story — it’s us.”

Last year, the U.N. established what it says is the world’s first independent international scientific panel on A.I. It issued a preliminary report in July.

“I’m afraid it’s a depressing read,” said one member of the panel, Prof. Sonia Livingstone, director of the Digital Futures for Children center at the London School of Economics and Political Science.

Though she acknowledged the “excitement about A.I.,” she noted that the technology has already been linked to “a litany of problems.” These include a proliferation of child sexual abuse material, “deep fakes” used in pornography, sycophantic chatbots that reinforce misleading beliefs and the mass production of baseless content that erodes public trust in the information ecosystem.

“Most harms fall disproportionately on disadvantaged people,” Professor Livingstone said.

On Monday, her panel released a brief analyzing a recent incident that has fanned the flames of the current firestorm. This summer, the company OpenAI said that automated agents had joined forces and hacked the A.I. infrastructure of another company, Hugging Face.

The “incident is an early warning of one possible route to more severe future loss of control,” the panel wrote. The hack, it said, highlights how A.I. agents could pursue “a goal that goes beyond or even conflicts with human intentions.”

The panel offered no quick fixes.

“The best response is still under debate,” it said. But it warned that the threat “requires far greater attention and resources.”

Since OpenAI’s disclosure, another major artificial intelligence company, Anthropic, has also said its A.I. agents had hacked other companies. And on Friday, Google revealed that its system, Gemini, escaped its testing environment in May and hacked several businesses.

These episodes suggest that artificial intelligence development could outpace its makers’ ability to understand the tools, prompting even some industry leaders to call for a paced approach to growth.

President Trump, who will address the General Assembly on Tuesday, has rejected the notion of deliberately slowing the development of A.I. But on Saturday he said he would create an A.I. force and appoint an A.I. czar. It is not clear what this force might do, but Mr. Trump said it would not hinder industry growth.

A.I. is likely to be back on the agenda on Wednesday, when Mr. Trump is expected to meet with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington.

Even as the U.N. focused on the worst-case scenarios presented by A.I., some at the digital cooperation conference called attention to the problems that already exist.

Roxana Minzatu, the European Commission’s executive vice president on social rights and jobs, said there was not enough understanding, or discussion, of how reliance on A.I. tools will affect education, jobs, critical thinking and more.

“This conversation is only now starting,” she said. “But I don’t know how much time we have.”

item.title: Iraq’s Prime Minister Vows to Disarm and Disband Iran-backed Militias in 2027
item.description:
Iraq’s prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, pledged to disarm his country’s Iran-backed militias by June 2027, laying out an exceptionally ambitious timeline for bringing the country’s unwieldy array of militants under state control.

The phased disarmament plan, which Mr. al-Zaidi laid out for the first time in an interview with The New York Times on Saturday in Baghdad, would be central to how Iraq manages the delicate balancing act between its two most important allies, the United States and Iran, at a time when those countries are at war.

Iraq is under mounting pressure from the Trump administration, its most critical security and economic partner, to defang the Iran-aligned forces, which have accrued not only military might, but also political power. At the same time, Iran, Iraq’s neighbor, is seeking to deepen its influence in the country and expand the use of those militias in the war with Washington.

Disarming the militias has bedeviled previous Iraqi leaders, including those with far more experience than Mr. al-Zaidi in the country’s fractious political scene. Iran-backed factions have become increasingly entrenched over recent years, forming parties that are enmeshed in Iraq’s political and economic system and making their containment a daunting task.

“This is not something that is optional. It is a necessity,” Mr. al-Zaidi said of his disarmament plan, in his first interview with foreign news media at his official residence. “Others who spoke of this then backtracked,” he said. “They yielded to pressure or to other concerns. For me, this issue, along with that of corruption, is a matter of honor.”

The difficulties have not deterred Mr. al-Zaidi, who was a political novice before becoming prime minister this year. Before his nomination, the wealthy businessman was largely unknown to most Iraqis.

This week, as Mr. al-Zaidi will attend his first United Nations General Assembly, he is confronting not only a security challenge, but also a daunting economic crisis.

Iraq, the world’s third-largest supplier of oil, has lost 60 percent of its monthly export revenue because of the war between the United States and Iran, which has choked off shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Mr. al-Zaidi said. Since taking office, he has been pitching proposals to build pipelines that would bypass the Persian Gulf, including one that he said could reach Europe.

“We wish to build bridges and economic ties between Iraq and the countries of the world,” he said. “Under this government, Iraq will be a meeting point, not a point of hostility.”

Realizing these aspirations, however, will depend on Mr. al-Zaidi’s meeting the Trump administration’s demand that he rein in the militias.

“Arms have to be confined first so you can build a solid economy,” he said.

Mr. al-Zaidi initially announced in the summer that the militias would be disarmed by the time the last remaining U.S. forces in Iraq withdraw on Sept. 30. Iraqi militias immediately rejected that timeline. After that, officials tried to correct what was seen in Iraq as a political blunder, saying instead that disarmament could begin Sept. 30.

Mr. al-Zaidi’s government has since formed a committee to negotiate with the militias over disarmament. He said the terms of the agreement on the timeline would be announced on Sept. 30.

According to Mr. al-Zaidi, there would first be a 90-day period during which the militias would not launch any attacks and be assured that they would not be attacked by U.S. forces. After that, the militias would begin handing over their weapons, with disarmament ending by June 30, 2027, he said, though the militias are still pushing to have until the end of 2027 to disarm.

Regional diplomats and some Iraqi security officials warn the timeline is extremely precarious. Most described it as nearly impossible to meet during a time of war, when Iran’s militia allies have proved valuable partners in sowing regional chaos and helping impose drastic costs on the global economy.

The militias have struck repeatedly at neighboring Kuwait and Jordan, as well as energy sites in Iraq and the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad.

This month, Saudi Arabia accused Iraq of being the source of a drone attack that knocked out the operation of the kingdom’s east-west pipeline, which provides 4 percent of global oil supplies. Iraqi officials believe splinter cells of the Iraqi militias helped operatives facilitate, though not orchestrate, that attack.

“The Iraqi government has stated that they’re not part of this war,” said Victoria Taylor, director of the Iraq Initiative at the Washington-based Atlantic Council. “But they don’t really have control over that.”

Iran would not greenlight the disarming of its Iraqi allies, she said, at a time when they have proved themselves to be “an extremely potent tool.”

A senior Iraqi security official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations with militias, warned that although some U.S. officials seemed receptive to Mr. al-Zaidi’s timeline, the plan would fail without a peace deal between the United States and Iran. That is still nowhere in sight.

Beyond the geopolitics, disarming Iraq’s militias could prove difficult because they have become so numerous and diffuse.

After U.S. forces invaded Iraq in 2003 and toppled its dictator, Saddam Hussein, several militant groups from Iran’s Shiite Muslim majority emerged to fight the U.S. occupation, often with training and arms from Iran, the region’s Shiite power.

Then, in 2014, the Sunni jihadist group the Islamic State launched an offensive that at its height seized more than a third of Iraqi territory. While awaiting help from a U.S.-led military coalition, Iraq announced a mobilization of forces. Countless new armed groups were formed, many under Iranian direction.

Iraq’s government has tried since then to rein in these militias — collectively called the Popular Mobilization Forces, or P.M.F. — and place them under state authority. Even those who have come under the state, however, maintain deep ties with Tehran and other Iran-backed militias outside state control.

The government’s current efforts are focused on four powerful militias that have resisted calls to disarm or come under the state.

Mr. al-Zaidi said his goal is for these militias to cease to exist as independent entities. “They will join the Popular Mobilization Forces as individuals and integrate into them,” he said. After the deadline, he said, any groups operating under militia names “will be deemed outlaws.”

These main groups insist they have the right to bear arms as long as “occupying forces” pose a threat, and point to the war the United States and Israel launched on Iran in February. The groups argue that U.S. forces and Israel, which built covert bases in the Iraqi desert, are using Iraq’s territory.

Ramzy Mardini, the founder of Geopol Labs, a Middle East-based geopolitical risk advisory firm, said a successful disarmament timeline required not only an easing of the regional conflict but a government that could enforce its demands and offer incentives or assurances to armed factions that comply.

“Until there are real changes in the political and security context, a deadline is merely an aspiration,” he said.

As the final U.S. troop withdrawal has neared, militias have raised additional conditions for their disarmament. The groups, for example, have pointed to the continued presence of Turkish troops in northern Iraq. Turkey has said it must maintain forces in Iraq to fight Turkish Kurdish separatist militants on its borders. In response, Mr. al-Zaidi said he has sought a deal with Turkey for its withdrawal.

In the past, Turkey has said any withdrawal is conditional on Kurdish militants’ camps and weapons being cleared from northern Iraq. Mr. al-Zaidi said his government was also working on a timeline to absorb local Kurdish forces into Iraq’s P.M.F. to satisfy that demand.

In pursuit of a deal with Turkey, Mr. al-Zaidi said he had leveraged Iraq’s efforts at boosting economic ties between the countries. This year, Iraq agreed to a one-year deal to increase oil exports to Turkey via an existing Iraqi pipeline, and Iraq now aims to increase the pipeline’s capacity, he said. Last week, during visits to France and Germany, he proposed plans to build pipelines via Turkey that would bring Iraqi oil directly to Europe.

During the interview, Mr. al-Zaidi also detailed some of the economic challenges his country now faced. Iraq has lost approximately $60 billion in revenues since the war began, he said.

Although Iraq considers itself a regional partner with Iran, he said, Iran has not allowed Iraqi tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

“We spoke at length. The decision emerging from Iran is firm,” he added. “Their goal is to drive up global oil prices. This is not about being close to them or not. Regardless, they want to create pressure.”
